Outpatient exercise echo would be correct only after a confirmed rule-out with low-risk discharge pathway (Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS).

explanation.summary: The 0/1 hour high-sensitivity troponin algorithm rules out NSTEMI if the baseline value is very low (less than 5 ng/L for hs-cTnI) and chest pain onset was more than 3 hours ago, or if the 1-hour delta is below a defined threshold. Rule-in requires either a baseline above the rule-in cut-off (greater than 52 ng/L) or a 1-hour delta above the rule-in delta (greater than 6 ng/L). All others fall into the observe zone and need a 3-hour repeat plus further risk stratification.
key_points: 0/1h algorithm: rule-out, rule-in, or observe
Observe zone: repeat at 3h + CTCA or stress testing
Rule-in delta cut-offs are assay-specific - read your lab
Fibrinolysis is contraindicated in NSTE-ACS
Invasive angiography in NSTEMI: less than 2h if high-risk, less than 24h if intermediate
explanation.pearls: An 'observe zone' troponin pattern is not reassurance - it's a mandate for further workup.

stem:
A 67-year-old man presents with 2 hours of severe central chest pain radiating to the back, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. He has a history of hypertension on amlodipine and a 40 pack-year smoking history. He has no prior cardiac history. On arrival he is in pain, clammy and pale. The 12-lead ECG shows horizontal ST depression of 2 mm in V1, V2 and V3 with prominent upright R-waves in V1 and V2 (R/S greater than 1), tall upright T waves in V1 to V3, and no ST elevation or depression in any other lead.

There is no Q-wave. A posterior 15-lead ECG with leads V7, V8 and V9 placed below the left scapula shows 1 mm ST elevation in V8 and V9. Troponin I is pending. Bedside echocardiogram shows inferolateral wall hypokinesis. The ED registrar asks whether to manage as NSTEMI with conservative pathway and 24-hour angiography, whether the ECG could represent Wellens syndrome, right bundle branch block, or digoxin effect, and whether emergency cath lab activation is justified for a STEMI equivalent in the absence of overt ST elevation on the standard 12-lead.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, JVP not elevated, chest clear, dual heart sounds no murmur.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 2 mm horizontal ST depression V1 to V3, dominant R in V1/V2, upright T waves. Posterior leads V8, V9: 1 mm ST elevation.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Manage as NSTEMI with conservative pathway and angiography within 24 hours
options.rationale: The 24-hour NSTEMI window does not apply when posterior leads confirm STEMI equivalent. This is the most common posterior STEMI miss - treating it as NSTEMI because there is only ST depression anteriorly. This pathway would be correct only with negative posterior leads and rise/fall biomarker pattern consistent with NSTEMI (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; ANZCOR).

options.text: Activate the cath lab for emergency primary PCI as a STEMI equivalent
options.rationale: Isolated posterior STEMI presents with ST depression in V1 to V3 (reciprocal), dominant R in V1, and is confirmed by ST elevation greater than 0.5 mm in posterior leads V7 to V9. It carries equivalent prognosis to anterior STEMI and mandates emergency reperfusion within the standard PPCI window (Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS Guideline; eTG Cardiovascular).

options.text: Treat as Wellens syndrome with urgent outpatient cardiology referral
options.rationale: Wellens syndrome shows biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2 to V3 in a pain-free patient with prior chest pain (a critical proximal LAD lesion sign); this ECG shows reciprocal ST depression with upright T and posterior ST elevation, not Wellens morphology. Wellens management is urgent inpatient angiography, not emergency PCI activation (LITFL; Heart Foundation).

options.text: Diagnose right bundle branch block and arrange echocardiogram in the morning
options.rationale: RBBB shows an rSR pattern in V1 with a broad QRS (>=120 ms) and discordant T-wave inversion; this ECG has a narrow QRS with dominant R and upright T - the wrong morphology. The anti-pattern is anchoring on dominant R in V1 without checking QRS width (Heart Foundation; LITFL).

options.text: Diagnose digoxin effect and check digoxin level urgently
options.rationale: Digoxin effect shows scooped (Salvador Dali moustache) ST depression with shortened QT, typically in lateral leads, in patients on digoxin. He is not on digoxin and the pattern is acute ischaemic. This would only be correct in a digoxin-treated patient with the classic scooped morphology (AMH).

explanation.summary: Isolated posterior STEMI is missed on the standard 12-lead because the infarct vector points away from the anterior precordial leads. Recognising horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with dominant upright R-waves and upright T-waves should prompt a posterior 15-lead ECG; ST elevation greater than 0.5 mm in V7 to V9 confirms posterior STEMI, which is a STEMI equivalent requiring emergency PPCI.
key_points: Posterior STEMI: ST depression V1-V3, dominant R V1/V2, upright T V1-V3
Confirm with posterior leads V7, V8, V9 (less than 1 mm threshold: 0.5 mm)
Most commonly from circumflex or dominant RCA occlusion
STEMI-equivalent: emergency PPCI within standard window
Other STEMI equivalents: LBBB with Sgarbossa criteria, aVR elevation with diffuse ST depression
explanation.pearls: Anterior ST depression with dominant R-wave is posterior STEMI until proven otherwise - flip the ECG upside down and backwards to see the elevation.

subtopic_detail: Posterior STEMI - ECG recognition with isolated ST depression in V1 to V3

stem:
A 62-year-old woman undergoes successful primary PCI with a single drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD for an anterior STEMI. She has hypertension on perindopril, dyslipidaemia, no diabetes, and no prior bleeding. Pre-procedure haemoglobin was 138 g/L and platelets 240 x 10^9/L. She was loaded with aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor 180 mg in the ED. Post-procedurally she is haemodynamically stable, has no ongoing chest pain, and an echocardiogram shows an LVEF of 42 percent with anteroseptal hypokinesis.

She has no history of stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, peptic ulcer disease, or anticoagulant use. The cardiology team plans discharge on day 3. She has private cover and no PBS concerns about device or drug choice.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, dual heart sounds, no signs of heart failure.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132 g/L, platelets 232 x 10^9/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, LVEF 42 percent.
data_table.Medications: Loaded with aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor 180 mg; ramipril 5 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg started inpatient.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate ongoing antiplatelet regimen?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily plus ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily for 12 months, then aspirin alone indefinitely
options.rationale: Default DAPT post-ACS-PCI is aspirin 100 mg daily plus ticagrelor 90 mg BD for 12 months (or prasugrel as an alternative), then aspirin alone indefinitely, unless bleeding risk dictates otherwise (Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS Guideline; eTG Cardiovascular).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 12 months, then aspirin alone
options.rationale: Clopidogrel is the alternative P2Y12 when ticagrelor and prasugrel are contraindicated (high bleeding risk, prior intracranial bleed, on long-term anticoagulation, ticagrelor dyspnoea intolerance). It is less potent than ticagrelor (PLATO showed superior outcomes for ticagrelor). This would be correct as default only when ticagrelor/prasugrel are contraindicated (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; AMH).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily alone, with clopidogrel added only if recurrent ischaemia occurs
options.rationale: Single antiplatelet post-ACS-PCI substantially increases stent thrombosis risk; DAPT for at least 12 months is standard. This would be correct only after the planned DAPT duration is completed, or earlier if a major bleeding event mandates de-escalation (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily plus prasugrel 10 mg daily for 6 months, then aspirin alone
options.rationale: Prasugrel is an alternative to ticagrelor but is contraindicated with prior stroke/TIA, not recommended over age 75, and at reduced dose if under 60 kg. Default ACS-PCI duration is 12 months, not 6 months. Six-month DAPT would be correct only with high bleeding risk after careful weighing (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; AMH).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily plus apixaban 5 mg twice daily for 12 months
options.rationale: DOAC plus aspirin is not standard post-ACS-PCI in sinus rhythm; this would be correct only if the patient had concurrent AF requiring anticoagulation, in which case triple therapy (DOAC + aspirin + clopidogrel) is given for the shortest possible period (typically 1 week to 1 month) then dual therapy with DOAC + clopidogrel (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; AMH).

explanation.summary: Default DAPT after ACS with PCI in Australia is aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 90 mg BD or prasugrel) for 12 months. Clopidogrel substitutes when more potent agents are contraindicated. Shorter or longer DAPT can be tailored to bleeding/ischaemic risk using validated scores (DAPT, PRECISE-DAPT).
key_points: Aspirin + ticagrelor (or prasugrel) x 12 months post-ACS-PCI
Clopidogrel if high bleeding risk, prior ICH, or on oral anticoagulant
Prasugrel: avoid if prior stroke/TIA, age greater than 75, weight less than 60 kg
Lifelong aspirin after DAPT period unless contraindicated
Tailor with DAPT/PRECISE-DAPT scores
explanation.pearls: Ticagrelor causes dyspnoea in about 1 in 7 patients - reassure but do not stop unless severe.

subtopic_detail: ACS - DAPT choice and duration post-PCI

stem:
A 74-year-old man with known HFrEF (LVEF 32 percent) presents to the ED with 2 days of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and 3 kg weight gain. He admits to non-adherence with his furosemide for 1 week. He has a background of ischaemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, and CKD stage 3 (baseline creatinine 140 micromol/L). On arrival he is sitting upright, working hard to breathe, and unable to complete sentences.

He has bibasal crackles to the mid-zones and elevated JVP. He has no chest pain and his ECG shows old anterior Q-waves without acute ischaemic changes. His usual medications are furosemide 40 mg BD, perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, and dapagliflozin 10 mg. The team specifically asks whether IV fluid bolus and IV metoprolol for the tachycardia would help, whether IV morphine with high-flow nasal cannula at 60 L/min is appropriate, whether to withhold his ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker indefinitely while starting dobutamine, and whether oral diuretics would suffice.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/94 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 88% RA improving to 94% on 6 L Hudson, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, accessory muscle use, bibasal crackles to mid-zones, JVP 8 cm, peripheral oedema to mid-shins.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: SR with old anterior Q-waves. Troponin I 28 ng/L (cut-off less than 16). NT-proBNP 4200 ng/L. Creatinine 175 micromol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Furosemide 40 mg BD, perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV furosemide 80 mg bolus, GTN infusion, and non-invasive ventilation with CPAP
options.rationale: Acute pulmonary oedema with hypertensive blood pressure and severe respiratory distress is managed with IV loop diuretic (typically 1 to 2.5 times the home oral dose), IV nitrate to reduce preload/afterload, and non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) to reduce work of breathing and improve oxygenation (Heart Foundation/CSANZ HF Guideline 2018; eTG Cardiovascular).

options.text: IV fluid bolus 500 mL Hartmann's and IV metoprolol 5 mg for the tachycardia
options.rationale: Fluid loading worsens pulmonary oedema in an already congested patient; IV beta-blockade in acute decompensation precipitates cardiogenic shock by removing residual sympathetic compensation. This combination would never be correct in ADHF; it would be appropriate only if the diagnosis were misread as septic tachyarrhythmia without congestion (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; AMH).

options.text: IV morphine 5 mg with high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 60 L/min and observation
options.rationale: Routine opioid use in ADHF is associated with worse outcomes (increased mortality, ICU admission, intubation) and is no longer recommended - a key legacy anti-pattern. HFNO has not been shown superior to NIV in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Morphine is reserved at most for terminal palliative dyspnoea (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).

options.text: Withhold his ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker indefinitely and start a dobutamine infusion
options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for cardiogenic shock with hypotension and end-organ hypoperfusion; this patient is hypertensive and not in shock. Chronic disease-modifying therapy (ACEi, beta-blocker) should generally be continued during decompensation unless hypotension or AKI dictates otherwise. Indefinite withdrawal worsens long-term outcomes (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).

options.text: Oral furosemide 80 mg, oral metolazone 5 mg, and admit to a monitored bed
options.rationale: Oral diuretic onset is too slow for acute severe pulmonary oedema with respiratory failure (gut oedema impairs absorption); IV diuretic is required. Oral diuresis is appropriate only in stable congestion managed in clinic or after acute response, not as initial management in respiratory distress (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; AMH).

explanation.summary: Acute pulmonary oedema with respiratory failure and elevated BP is managed with IV loop diuretic, IV nitrate, and non-invasive ventilation. Inotropes are restricted to cardiogenic shock. Routine morphine is now avoided. Chronic disease-modifying therapy (beta-blocker, RAAS inhibitor) is generally continued at reduced dose where tolerated.
key_points: IV furosemide dose: 1 to 2.5 x oral home dose
GTN reduces preload and afterload - useful if BP is preserved
NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) reduces intubation rate in cardiogenic APO
Inotropes only if hypotensive with end-organ hypoperfusion
Avoid routine morphine - increased mortality signal
explanation.pearls: Hypertensive flash pulmonary oedema needs nitrates more than it needs diuretics - venous redistribution buys minutes.

subtopic_detail: Acute decompensated heart failure - initial management priorities

stem:
A 66-year-old woman with HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent, ischaemic aetiology) attends the heart failure clinic. She is NYHA class II to III with mild exertional dyspnoea climbing one flight. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.2 percent), hypertension, and CKD stage 3a (eGFR 52, baseline). She has been on stable doses for 3 months of perindopril 8 mg daily, bisoprolol 7.5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 80 mg.

Her BP is 118/72 mmHg, HR 64 bpm, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L. She has no symptomatic hypotension. She is keen to optimise prognosis-modifying therapy and has private cover for medication cost. She specifically asks whether to add digoxin for prognosis, whether to increase her furosemide and add amlodipine for blood pressure, whether to refer for cardiac resynchronisation now, or whether to switch to candesartan with ivabradine instead of the ARNI and MRA approach. She has private cover and PBS access to all four pillars.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 64 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: JVP not elevated, chest clear, dual heart sounds with soft S3, trace ankle oedema.
data_table.Investigations: LVEF 28 percent. eGFR 52, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.2 percent, NT-proBNP 980 ng/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 7.5 mg, furosemide 40 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step to optimise prognosis?

options.text: Add spironolactone 25 mg daily and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, and plan switch of perindopril to sacubitril/valsartan after a 36-hour washout
options.rationale: The four pillars of HFrEF GDMT are ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor; she is already on ACEi and beta-blocker and needs the remaining two pillars added, with ACEi-to-ARNI switch (after 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema) for additional mortality benefit (Heart Foundation/CSANZ HF Guideline; eTG Cardiovascular).

options.text: Add digoxin 125 micrograms daily as the next prognostic agent, continuing perindopril and bisoprolol at their current doses
options.rationale: Digoxin reduces HF hospitalisations but has no mortality benefit and is not a prognosis pillar; the anti-pattern is reaching for digoxin before completing four-pillar GDMT. Digoxin would be reasonable for persistent symptoms on full GDMT, particularly with concurrent AF requiring additional rate control (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; AMH).

options.text: Increase furosemide to 80 mg daily and add amlodipine 5 mg daily for tighter blood pressure control without adding any additional prognosis-modifying agent
options.rationale: Loop diuretics are symptom-controlling not prognosis-modifying; amlodipine is neutral in HFrEF but does not improve survival. The anti-pattern is escalating non-prognostic therapy while skipping the mortality-reducing pillars. Diuretic escalation is correct for symptomatic congestion, not asymptomatic LV dysfunction (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).

options.text: Refer for cardiac resynchronisation therapy now, given the persistent NYHA class II to III symptoms on her current triple-therapy regimen
options.rationale: CRT is indicated for LVEF <=35% with LBBB and QRS >=130 ms after at least 3 months of optimised GDMT; she has not had GDMT optimised first. CRT before four-pillar optimisation misses the reverse-remodelling benefit and risks inappropriate device implantation if LVEF recovers (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).

options.text: Switch perindopril to candesartan 8 mg daily and add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily for additional symptomatic and prognostic benefit in HFrEF management
options.rationale: Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm with HR >=77 bpm on maximally tolerated beta-blocker (SHIFT trial threshold); her HR is 64 bpm so she does not qualify. ARB substitutes for ACEi only when ACEi-intolerant (cough, angioedema), not as a routine switch. This option mixes two off-target choices (Heart Foundation/CSANZ; SHIFT).

explanation.summary: Modern HFrEF GDMT comprises four prognosis pillars: ACE inhibitor or ARNI, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor. All four should be initiated and titrated in parallel where tolerated. ARNI switch from ACEi requires a 36-hour washout to reduce angioedema risk. Diuretics are symptom-controlling and do not improve survival.
key_points: Four pillars: ACEi/ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i
ARNI: 36 h washout from ACEi to avoid angioedema
SGLT2i benefit independent of diabetes status
Monitor potassium and renal function with MRA + ACEi/ARNI
CRT after at least 3 months of optimised GDMT if QRS criteria met
explanation.pearls: Start the SGLT2 inhibitor early - the survival curves separate within weeks, not years.

subtopic_detail: Chronic HFrEF - guideline-directed medical therapy escalation

stem:
A 68-year-old woman is referred for symptomatic palpitations and exertional dyspnoea over the past 3 weeks. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 118 bpm at rest. She has hypertension on perindopril, no diabetes, no prior stroke, and no heart failure. Her LVEF on echo done last week is 58 percent with a mildly dilated left atrium (44 mm) and no significant valvular disease.

She is otherwise active and reports the palpitations are interfering with her hiking. Her current symptom burden is EHRA class IIb. Her TSH and electrolytes are normal. She specifically asks whether rate control alone is acceptable, whether early electrical cardioversion is preferred, whether anticoagulation alone is sufficient pending spontaneous reversion, whether digoxin monotherapy without anticoagulation would be appropriate given her age, or whether amiodarone loading without anticoagulation is reasonable in someone with such low overall stroke risk.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 118 bpm irregular, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, dual heart sounds no murmur, chest clear, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF with rate 118. Echo: LVEF 58 percent, LA 44 mm. TSH 2.1 mIU/L, K 4.0 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management strategy for her atrial fibrillation?

options.text: Rate control only with bisoprolol, with rhythm control reserved for two or more recurrences after rate-control optimisation
options.rationale: In symptomatic AF of recent onset (<1 year), early rhythm control reduces cardiovascular events compared with rate control alone (EAST-AFNET 4). The 'wait for recurrences' approach is the pre-EAST-AFNET legacy practice. Rate-control-only would be correct in long-standing persistent AF (>1 year), asymptomatic patients, or patients who decline rhythm interventions (CSANZ AF Guideline 2018; EAST-AFNET 4).

options.text: Commence apixaban and a rate-controlling beta-blocker, then refer for early electrical cardioversion with consideration of catheter ablation
options.rationale: Symptomatic AF within 12 months of diagnosis benefits from an early rhythm-control strategy (cardioversion plus antiarrhythmic or ablation), with appropriate anticoagulation based on CHA2DS2-VA score; she meets criteria (symptomatic, recent onset, suitable candidate) (CSANZ AF Guideline; eTG; EAST-AFNET 4).

options.text: Anticoagulation alone with apixaban; AF often spontaneously reverts without further intervention
options.rationale: She is symptomatic (EHRA IIb) and tachycardic at 118; anticoagulation alone is insufficient. Spontaneous reversion happens but should not be relied on. Anticoagulation alone would be appropriate only in asymptomatic permanent AF with rate already controlled (CSANZ AF).

options.text: Digoxin monotherapy for rate control without anticoagulation as her CHA2DS2-VA score is 1
options.rationale: Digoxin monotherapy is poor for exertional rate control (vagal action diminished by sympathetic activity) and her CHA2DS2-VA is 2 (age 65 to 74 = 1, female = 1, hypertension = 1 - actually 3), meeting the threshold for anticoagulation. The combined errors make this never correct (CSANZ AF).

options.text: Amiodarone loading orally for 4 weeks followed by maintenance, with no anticoagulation given low stroke risk
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is required regardless of antiarrhythmic strategy when CHA2DS2-VA reaches threshold; rhythm control does not abolish stroke risk. Amiodarone is generally reserved for structural heart disease or failed first-line antiarrhythmics due to long-term toxicity (thyroid, lung, hepatic, ocular). This would only be appropriate in structural heart disease with failed flecainide/sotalol AND with anticoagulation (CSANZ AF; AMH).

explanation.summary: Symptomatic AF diagnosed within the past 12 months should be considered for early rhythm control (cardioversion, antiarrhythmics, or catheter ablation) alongside anticoagulation, as this reduces cardiovascular events compared with rate control alone (EAST-AFNET 4 incorporated into CSANZ guidance). Anticoagulation is governed by CHA2DS2-VA, not by rhythm vs rate strategy.
key_points: Early rhythm control improves outcomes in recent-onset symptomatic AF
Anticoagulation is independent of rate vs rhythm strategy
CHA2DS2-VA replaces CHA2DS2-VASc in Australia (drops sex modifier)
Catheter ablation first-line for paroxysmal AF in suitable candidates
Amiodarone reserved for structural heart disease or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: EAST-AFNET 4 shifted the paradigm - rhythm-control benefits accrue when started within the first year, not after years of failed rate control.

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation - rate vs rhythm control strategy

stem: A 76-year-old woman with newly diagnosed persistent non-valvular atrial fibrillation attends a cardiology clinic. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on amlodipine, and a transient ischaemic attack 3 years ago with full recovery. She has CKD stage 3b with creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m2, and weighs 58 kg. Her haemoglobin is 122 g/L, platelets 230 x 10^9/L, and she has no history of GI bleeding or peptic ulcer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 82 bpm irregular, RR 14.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, chest clear, no neurological deficit, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m2, weight 58 kg, Hb 122 g/L, platelets 230 x 10^9/L, ALT/AST normal.
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, amlodipine 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA = 6 (age greater than or equal to 75 = 2, diabetes = 1, hypertension = 1, prior TIA = 2). Apixaban dose-reduction criteria require any 2 of: age greater than or equal to 80, weight less than or equal to 60 kg, creatinine greater than or equal to 133 micromol/L. She meets weight and creatinine criteria, so 2.5 mg BD is correct (CSANZ AF Guideline; AMH).

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely
options.rationale: She meets two apixaban dose-reduction criteria (weight 58 kg <=60 kg, and creatinine 138 micromol/L >=133 micromol/L) - any two of the three triggers the 2.5 mg BD dose. Standard 5 mg BD would lead to over-anticoagulation. This dose would be correct only with at most one reduction criterion (AMH; CSANZ AF).

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily indefinitely
options.rationale: Dabigatran is ~80% renally cleared and is contraindicated in Australia with CrCl <30 mL/min per AMH. eGFR 32 puts her at borderline and she lacks the renal margin apixaban provides. Dabigatran 150 mg BD would be appropriate only with stable CrCl >=50 mL/min in younger patients without bleeding risk (AMH; CSANZ AF).

options.text: Warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely
options.rationale: Warfarin is acceptable but not preferred for non-valvular AF; DOACs (especially apixaban) have lower intracranial bleeding rates and avoid INR monitoring. Warfarin is the correct choice for mechanical valves, moderate-severe mitral stenosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, severe CKD/dialysis, or where DOACs are contraindicated/unavailable (CSANZ AF).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF (ACTIVE-W trial showed this clearly). This is a key legacy anti-pattern of substituting antiplatelets for anticoagulation. DAPT for AF stroke prevention is essentially never correct (CSANZ AF; ACTIVE-W).

explanation.summary: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation hinges on a structured risk assessment with the CHA2DS2-VA score (Australian convention dropping the sex modifier from CHA2DS2-VASc) and bleeding-risk balance with HAS-BLED. Score 1 or more in men or 2 or more in women indicates anticoagulation. DOACs (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban) are preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AF because of comparable or superior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage, no INR monitoring, and fewer drug-food interactions. Choice between DOACs depends on renal function, weight, age, and patient preference. Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BD if any 2 of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or under, or creatinine 133 micromol/L or above. Dabigatran 110 mg BD for age over 80 or eGFR 30-50; avoid all DOACs in eGFR under 15. Warfarin remains first-line for mechanical valves and moderate or severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin has no role in AF stroke prevention.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA: CHF 1, HTN 1, Age 65-74 1 or greater than or equal to 75 2, DM 1, Stroke/TIA 2, Vasc 1
Apixaban dose-reduce if any 2 of age greater than or equal to 80, weight less than or equal to 60 kg, Cr greater than or equal to 133
Dabigatran contraindicated CrCl less than 30 mL/min
Rivaroxaban dose-reduce to 15 mg if CrCl 15-49
Warfarin remains required for mechanical valves and moderate-severe MS
explanation.pearls: Apixaban dose reduction to 2.5 mg BD in non-valvular AF requires any 2 of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or under, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above. CHA2DS2-VA (no sex modifier in Australian practice) score 1 or more in men or 2 or more in women indicates anticoagulation (NHFA/CSANZ; AMH).

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation - CHA2DS2-VA scoring and DOAC selection

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden palpitations for 50 minutes. She has had similar self-terminating episodes since her teens. She is haemodynamically stable. Her past history includes moderate persistent asthma managed with budesonide-formoterol; she had a hospital admission with status asthmaticus 3 years ago and reports wheeze with viral illnesses. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and drinks 2 to 3 coffees daily.

On arrival she is anxious but well perfused. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 184 bpm with no clearly visible P waves and a normal QRS axis. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre with leg elevation has been attempted twice without success.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 184 bpm regular, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Warm well-perfused peripheries, GCS 15, chest clear, no signs of heart failure.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: narrow-complex regular tachycardia 184 bpm, no clear P waves, normal axis. K 4.2 mmol/L, TSH normal.
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV adenosine 6 mg rapid push followed by 20 mL saline flush with continuous ECG recording
options.rationale: Adenosine is normally first-line after failed vagal manoeuvres in stable narrow-complex SVT, but it can precipitate severe bronchospasm and is relatively contraindicated in patients with significant active asthma (eTG Cardiovascular; AMH).

options.text: IV verapamil 5 mg slowly over 2 minutes with continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring
options.rationale: In stable narrow-complex SVT where adenosine is relatively contraindicated by active asthma, IV verapamil (or diltiazem) is the preferred alternative provided LV function is preserved and the rhythm is genuinely narrow-complex (eTG Cardiovascular; AMH).

options.text: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 50 joules under procedural sedation with continuous monitoring
options.rationale: Synchronised cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamically unstable SVT (hypotension, shock, ischaemia, severe heart failure); she remains stable so pharmacological termination is preferred (ANZCOR 11.10).

options.text: Oral metoprolol 25 mg with discharge home and cardiology outpatient follow-up if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Oral beta-blockade does not acutely terminate SVT and discharge in active tachyarrhythmia is unsafe; non-selective beta-blockade also risks bronchospasm in asthma (ANZCOR; eTG).

options.text: IV amiodarone 300 mg loading dose over 60 minutes via a peripheral large-bore cannula
options.rationale: Amiodarone is reserved for wide-complex tachycardia or refractory arrhythmias; it is not first-line for stable narrow-complex SVT and carries significant proarrhythmic and toxicity profile (ANZCOR; eTG).

explanation.summary: Stable narrow-complex SVT is treated with vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva preferred) followed by IV adenosine 6 mg, then 12 mg, then 12 mg if needed. Unstable SVT requires synchronised DC cardioversion. Verapamil or beta-blockers are alternatives in patients without contraindications.
key_points: Modified Valsalva (REVERT trial position) more effective than standard
Adenosine: 6 mg, 12 mg, 12 mg rapid push with saline flush
Warn patient about transient flushing/chest discomfort/sense of impending doom
Avoid adenosine in asthma (bronchospasm) and prefer alternatives
Unstable SVT: synchronised cardioversion 50 to 100 J
explanation.pearls: Always run a rhythm strip during adenosine - the brief AV block can unmask the underlying atrial activity (flutter waves, P-wave morphology).

stem:
A 72-year-old man presents with exertional dyspnoea, one episode of syncope while climbing stairs last week, and a 2-month history of chest tightness on hills. He has hypertension on amlodipine, hyperlipidaemia on atorvastatin, and is otherwise well. On auscultation there is an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotids, with a soft S2 and a slow-rising carotid pulse.

The murmur is intensity grade 3/6, peaks late in systole, and is louder on squatting. There is no S3, no opening snap, no MR jet, and no pulmonary congestion clinically. His ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern. CXR shows a borderline-enlarged cardiac silhouette without pulmonary oedema. He has never had an echocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/72 mmHg (narrow pulse pressure), HR 76 bpm regular, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: Slow-rising carotid pulse, soft S2, late-peaking ejection systolic murmur 3/6 RUSB radiating to carotids, louder on squatting. No S3. No mid-systolic click. JVP not elevated. No peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: LVH with strain. CXR: borderline cardiomegaly, clear lungs. Normal troponin and TSH.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly distinguishes severe aortic stenosis from hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy in this patient?

options.text: Murmur intensity increases on squatting and falls with Valsalva strain
options.rationale: In AS, increased venous return on squatting augments LV stroke volume and thus murmur intensity, whereas HOCM murmur diminishes on squatting (more LV filling reduces outflow tract obstruction). This dynamic response is the most reliable bedside discriminator (Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease; eTG Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease Statement

options.text: Presence of an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge today
options.rationale: Both AS and HOCM produce systolic murmurs in the precordial/parasternal area; location alone does not discriminate. AS classically radiates to carotids and HOCM does not, but mere presence at the right upper sternal edge is not diagnostic (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease Statement

options.text: ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy with associated strain pattern in lateral leads
options.rationale: LVH with strain occurs in both severe AS (pressure overload) and HCM (intrinsic hypertrophy); ECG cannot reliably differentiate them. The anti-pattern is using a non-specific finding to claim discrimination. LVH on ECG only confirms hypertrophy is present, not its cause (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease Statement

options.text: Exertional syncope as a presenting symptom in this elderly patient with murmur
options.rationale: Exertional syncope occurs in both severe AS and HOCM and is a high-risk red-flag in both; it cannot discriminate. Lead-pipe equivalence in symptoms is a classic teaching point for these two outflow obstructions (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease Statement

options.text: Presence of a slow-rising carotid pulse and a narrow pulse pressure today
options.rationale: Pulsus parvus et tardus does favour AS over HOCM (HOCM gives a bisferiens spike-and-dome pulse), but the question asks the STRONGEST discriminator. Dynamic squat/Valsalva manoeuvres are more specific and reproducible at the bedside than pulse character, which can be obscured by stiff vessels in older patients. Pulse character is supportive but not the strongest single sign (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease Statement

explanation.summary: Dynamic auscultation distinguishes fixed valvular outflow obstruction (AS) from dynamic LVOT obstruction (HOCM). Manoeuvres that decrease LV preload or afterload (Valsalva strain phase, standing) increase the HOCM murmur and decrease the AS murmur; manoeuvres that increase preload/afterload (squatting, handgrip) decrease the HOCM murmur and increase or maintain the AS murmur. Echocardiography confirms with peak velocity, mean gradient, AVA (severe AS: less than 1.0 cm2, peak velocity greater than or equal to 4 m/s, mean gradient greater than or equal to 40 mmHg).
key_points: AS murmur: louder with squatting, softer with Valsalva
HOCM murmur: softer with squatting, louder with Valsalva
Severe AS echo: AVA less than 1.0 cm2, peak velocity greater than or equal to 4 m/s, mean gradient greater than or equal to 40 mmHg
MR is holosystolic at apex radiating to axilla, with S3 if severe
Pulsus parvus et tardus favours AS but is insensitive in elderly with stiff vessels
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to squat then stand during your exam - the murmur change tells you the lesion before the echo does.

sources.label: Heart Foundation/CSANZ Valvular Heart Disease Statement

subtopic_detail: Valvular DDx - aortic stenosis vs HCM vs mitral regurgitation

stem:
A 68-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history attends his GP for review. Spirometry 4 weeks ago confirmed COPD with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58 and FEV1 62 percent predicted (GOLD 2). Over the past year he has had 2 exacerbations managed in the community with prednisolone and amoxicillin, and no hospital admissions. His mMRC dyspnoea score is 2 (stops for breath after about 100 m on the flat) and CAT score is 18.

He is currently on as-needed salbutamol inhaler only. He stopped smoking 6 months ago, is up to date with influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, and is enrolled in a pulmonary rehabilitation program. He has no diagnosis of asthma, no significant atopy, and a blood eosinophil count of 120 cells/microL. His GP specifically asks whether to add a LAMA alone, to add a fixed-dose LAMA/LABA combination, to add a LABA/ICS combination, to commence triple therapy with LAMA/LABA/ICS, or to add oral theophylline.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 95% RA.
data_table.Examination: Mild barrel chest, reduced air entry bilaterally, prolonged expiration, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Post-bronchodilator FEV1 62 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.58. Eosinophils 120 cells/microL. CXR hyperinflation without infiltrate.
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 100 microg pMDI PRN.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next inhaled therapy?

options.text: Add tiotropium 18 microg daily (LAMA)
options.rationale: Single long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA or LABA) is appropriate for low-symptom, low-exacerbation patients (mMRC <2, CAT <10, <1 exacerbation/year); he has both high symptom burden (mMRC 2, CAT 18) and 2 exacerbations in 12 months, mandating dual bronchodilation. This would be correct only as initial therapy in a less symptomatic, infrequent-exacerbator patient (Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X; GOLD).

options.text: Add a LAMA/LABA combination inhaler
options.rationale: Symptomatic COPD patients with exacerbations (greater than or equal to 2 moderate/year or any hospitalisation) and CAT greater than or equal to 10 should escalate from SABA to dual long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA/LABA) per Australian COPD-X; ICS is added only if eosinophils greater than or equal to 300 cells/microL or asthma overlap, and his eosinophils are 120 (Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X; eTG Respiratory).

options.text: Add a fixed-dose LABA/ICS combination
options.rationale: ICS adds pneumonia risk and should be reserved for patients with blood eosinophils >=300 cells/microL, asthma-COPD overlap, or persistent exacerbations on dual bronchodilator therapy. His eosinophils are 120. This option is the classic 'reach for ICS too early' anti-pattern. LABA/ICS would be appropriate only with eosinophilic phenotype or asthma overlap (COPD-X; GOLD).

options.text: Triple therapy with LAMA/LABA/ICS in a single inhaler
options.rationale: Triple therapy is escalation FROM dual bronchodilation when exacerbations persist; he has not trialled dual bronchodilator yet and lacks ICS-favouring features (eos <300, no asthma overlap). Triple therapy would be correct after dual bronchodilator failure with rising eosinophils or persistent exacerbations (COPD-X; GOLD).

options.text: Add oral theophylline 200 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, significant drug interactions (cytochrome P450), and limited efficacy; it is a last-line agent in stable COPD. Theophylline would only be considered after maximal inhaler therapy in patients with persistent symptoms and no other options (AMH; COPD-X).

explanation.summary: Australian COPD-X escalation is: SABA PRN, then LAMA or LABA monotherapy for low-symptom/low-exacerbation patients, then LAMA/LABA dual for higher symptom burden or exacerbators, then triple therapy (LAMA/LABA/ICS) for persistent exacerbators or those with eosinophilia or asthma overlap. Blood eosinophil count greater than or equal to 300 cells/microL favours ICS addition.
key_points: SABA PRN at all stages
LAMA or LABA monotherapy for mild symptomatic COPD
LAMA/LABA dual for greater than or equal to 2 exacerbations/year or high symptom burden
ICS adds pneumonia risk; eosinophil-guided (greater than or equal to 300) or ACO
Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehab provide the largest mortality benefits
explanation.pearls: Australian COPD-X is regularly updated by Lung Foundation Australia - check the latest version before deciding ICS escalation.

subtopic_detail: COPD - GOLD group classification and inhaler escalation

stem:
A 71-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 38 percent predicted) is brought to ED by ambulance with worsening dyspnoea, productive cough with greenish sputum, and confusion over the past 24 hours. She is a current smoker. On arrival she was placed on 8 L/min Hudson mask oxygen by paramedics; SpO2 is now 98 percent. She is drowsy with bounding peripheral pulses, flapping tremor, and warm sweaty palms.

She is using salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisers continuously since arrival. An arterial blood gas is taken on the current oxygen flow rate. Her usual inhalers are tiotropium and salmeterol/fluticasone, and she has had 3 prior admissions for COPD exacerbations in the past year, two requiring non-invasive ventilation. The ED registrar specifically asks whether to maintain current oxygen and proceed straight to intubation, to reduce oxygen to nasal prongs 2 L/min without ventilatory support, to administer IV doxapram to stimulate respiration, or to switch to nasal high-flow oxygen at 60 L/min and continue nebulisers as definitive management before any non-invasive ventilation trial is attempted. A BiPAP machine is available now in resus. ICU has been notified of likely admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/86 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 8 L Hudson mask, T 37.4 degC, GCS 13.
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, flapping tremor, warm peripheries, accessory muscle use, widespread polyphonic wheeze, prolonged expiration.
data_table.Investigations: ABG (on 8 L Hudson): pH 7.21, pCO2 88 mmHg, pO2 110 mmHg, HCO3 32 mmol/L, BE +3. CXR: hyperinflation, no consolidation or pneumothorax.
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium 18 microg daily, salmeterol/fluticasone 50/500 BD.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Titrate oxygen down to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92 percent and initiate non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP
options.rationale: She has acute on chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.21, pCO2 88) precipitated by hyperoxia; controlled oxygen to a target SpO2 88 to 92 percent and BiPAP (e.g. IPAP 12 to 15, EPAP 4 to 5) is the standard management for COPD with pH less than 7.35 despite optimal medical therapy (Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X; eTG Respiratory; BTS NIV).

options.text: Maintain the current 8 L/min Hudson mask oxygen flow rate and proceed straight to endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation
options.rationale: Intubation is for failure of NIV, severe agitation precluding mask tolerance, copious secretions, or cardiopulmonary arrest. Maintaining excessive oxygen (8 L Hudson mask drives the acidosis higher via Haldane effect and loss of hypoxic drive) compounds the harm. Intubation is correct only after NIV trial fails or contraindications to NIV exist (COPD-X; BTS NIV).

options.text: Reduce oxygen to nasal prongs at 2 L/min and observe in resus without ventilatory support pending repeat arterial blood gas in 1 hour
options.rationale: Reducing oxygen alone will not correct the respiratory acidosis quickly enough in a drowsy patient with pH 7.21 and pCO2 88; NIV is needed to actively unload CO2. Observation alone would be correct only with milder hypercapnia (pH >7.35) and adequate respiratory effort (COPD-X; BTS NIV).

options.text: Administer intravenous doxapram infusion to stimulate respiratory drive and continue current Hudson mask oxygen flow rate while awaiting ICU review
options.rationale: Doxapram is rarely used now and has been superseded by NIV; it causes agitation, arrhythmia, and seizure. Continued excessive oxygen compounds the problem. Doxapram has essentially no current role in COPD exacerbation management (AMH; BTS NIV).

options.text: Switch to nasal high-flow oxygen at 60 L/min, FiO2 0.6, and continue back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisers without BiPAP
options.rationale: Nasal high-flow oxygen can be used in selected COPD patients (HOT-AIR trial) but NIV (BiPAP) has stronger evidence and is first-line in hypercapnic respiratory failure with acidosis (pH <7.35). HFNO would be a reasonable second-line option if NIV is not tolerated, not the first-line choice with pH 7.21 (COPD-X; BTS NIV).

explanation.summary: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (Type 2) in COPD with pH less than 7.35 despite optimal pharmacological therapy is treated with BiPAP. Oxygen is titrated to target SpO2 88 to 92 percent to avoid worsening hypercapnia from loss of hypoxic drive and Haldane effect. Standard COPD exacerbation bundle: controlled oxygen, salbutamol + ipratropium nebs, prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days, antibiotics if increased purulence/dyspnoea/sputum volume.
key_points: Target SpO2 88-92% in COPD (avoid hyperoxia-induced CO2 retention)
NIV (BiPAP) for pH less than 7.35 with hypercapnia despite optimal therapy
Steroids: prednisolone 30-50 mg PO for 5 days
Antibiotics if Anthonisen criteria met: increased dyspnoea + sputum volume + sputum purulence
Intubation if NIV fails, GCS rapidly falling, or cardiopulmonary arrest
explanation.pearls: Bounding pulses, flap, and warm sweaty palms are the bedside triad of hypercapnia - they predict the ABG before it returns.

subtopic_detail: COPD exacerbation - acute management and ABG interpretation

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with known moderate persistent asthma presents to ED with 6 hours of progressively worsening dyspnoea, wheeze, and dry cough. She had a viral URTI 3 days ago. She has been using her salbutamol inhaler every 30 minutes for the last 2 hours with minimal relief. She has a background of eczema and rhinitis, no other medical history, and her usual inhaler is budesonide/formoterol 200/6 maintenance and reliever.

Her best-ever PEF is 460 L/min. On arrival she can only speak in short phrases, is sitting upright, and is using accessory muscles. There is widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze without focal crackles. There is no chest pain, no haemoptysis, and no calf swelling. The ED registrar asks specifically whether the exacerbation is mild-moderate, severe, or life-threatening, and which initial treatment bundle applies under the Australian Asthma Handbook for this patient today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 124 bpm, RR 30, SpO2 91% RA, T 37.0 degC.
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, accessory muscle use, short-phrase speech, widespread polyphonic wheeze, prolonged expiration.
data_table.Investigations: PEF 180 L/min (39 percent of personal best). CXR: hyperinflation, no consolidation/pneumothorax. K 3.6 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Budesonide/formoterol 200/6 BD maintenance and reliever.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate classification of severity and corresponding initial treatment?

options.text: Mild to moderate exacerbation - salbutamol pMDI 4 to 12 puffs via spacer and reassess in 20 minutes for ongoing wheeze
options.rationale: Mild to moderate asthma has PEF >60% of best, speaks in sentences, no accessory muscle use. Her PEF 39%, short-phrase speech, RR 30, SpO2 91% all meet severe criteria. The anti-pattern is under-classifying severity from a single number (e.g., looking only at SpO2). This management would only be appropriate in true mild-moderate exacerbation (Australian Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Severe exacerbation - continuous salbutamol nebulisers with ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone, and oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95 percent
options.rationale: Severe acute asthma in adults is defined by inability to complete sentences, PEF 40 to 60 percent of best, RR greater than or equal to 25, HR greater than or equal to 110, or SpO2 less than 92 percent; treatment is back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers, ipratropium, systemic corticosteroid, and controlled oxygen to SpO2 93 to 95 percent (Australian Asthma Handbook; eTG Respiratory).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Life-threatening exacerbation - immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation in the resus bay regardless of clinical response to bronchodilator therapy
options.rationale: Life-threatening features are silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, exhaustion, confusion, or PEF <33% - she does not yet meet these. Pre-emptive intubation in severe (not life-threatening) asthma without therapeutic trial increases morbidity; bronchospasm is best treated medically while preparing for escalation. Intubation is correct only after failed maximal medical therapy or imminent respiratory arrest (Australian Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Moderate exacerbation - oral prednisolone 50 mg and discharge home with safety-net advice and GP review in 24 hours for reassessment
options.rationale: Discharge without observation in a severe exacerbation is unsafe; she requires intensive bronchodilation, systemic steroid, and reassessment over hours to confirm response (typically 4-hour observation post stabilisation). Oral prednisolone discharge is correct for mild-moderate exacerbation after good response to inhaled bronchodilator in ED (Australian Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Severe exacerbation - IV magnesium sulfate 2 g as first-line and observe response before commencing salbutamol nebulisers or systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: IV magnesium 2 g over 20 minutes is a useful adjunct in severe asthma not responding to maximal first-line bronchodilation; it is not first-line. The anti-pattern is leading with adjunctive therapy. Magnesium is correct after 1 hour of continuous nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, and systemic steroid with inadequate response (Australian Asthma Handbook; eTG Respiratory).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Australian Asthma Handbook severity in adults uses speech, work of breathing, RR, HR, SpO2, and PEF percent best. Severe exacerbation criteria include any of: cannot complete sentences, accessory muscle use, RR greater than or equal to 25, HR greater than or equal to 110, SpO2 less than 92 percent, or PEF 40 to 60 percent of best. Treatment escalates from salbutamol pMDI plus spacer through nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, systemic corticosteroid, IV magnesium, and ICU referral for life-threatening features.
key_points: Severe: short-phrase speech, RR greater than or equal to 25, HR greater than or equal to 110, SpO2 less than 92, PEF 40 to 60 percent best
Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, PEF less than 33 percent
Steroids: prednisolone 50 mg PO or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
Target SpO2 93-95 percent (avoid over-oxygenation)
Magnesium 2 g IV over 20 min if severe and not responding
explanation.pearls: A normal pCO2 in a severe asthmatic is ominous - it signals fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

sources.label: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

stem:
A 31-year-old woman is reviewed by her GP for asthma. Over the past 3 months she has had daytime symptoms 3 to 4 times per week, nocturnal waking once weekly, and uses her salbutamol inhaler roughly 4 times per week. She has had no exacerbations requiring oral steroids in the past year. Her inhaler technique is excellent on observation. She is currently on salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI as needed only.

She is planning pregnancy in the next 6 months and asks specifically about whether she can keep using her reliever as her only inhaler in pregnancy. FEV1 is 88 percent predicted with bronchodilator reversibility of 14 percent. She has no rhinitis, reflux, or known occupational trigger.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no wheeze, no signs of allergic rhinitis.
data_table.Investigations: FEV1 88 percent predicted, BDR 14 percent, normal CXR.
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 100 microg pMDI PRN only.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue salbutamol PRN alone with a written asthma action plan and review after conception
options.rationale: Salbutamol-only therapy is no longer recommended at any step in adult asthma per the Australian Asthma Handbook (2024); her symptoms also meet criteria for poor control (SABA use greater than 2/week, nocturnal symptoms) and uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy carries higher fetal risk than ICS exposure.
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Commence low-dose budesonide-formoterol 200/6 used as anti-inflammatory reliever only with written action plan
options.rationale: Australian Asthma Handbook Step 1-2 adult therapy is low-dose ICS-formoterol as anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR); budesonide is the ICS with the strongest pregnancy safety data and formoterol is acceptable, so AIR is preferred ahead of conception over SABA-only or daily ICS plus SABA.
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Commence daily montelukast 10 mg nocte with continued salbutamol PRN as reliever
options.rationale: Leukotriene receptor antagonists are an add-on option in selected patients; they are inferior to ICS for first-line control and TGA has a boxed warning about neuropsychiatric effects, making montelukast an inappropriate first-line choice especially pre-conception.
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Commence high-dose fluticasone-salmeterol 500/50 twice daily with salbutamol PRN
options.rationale: High-dose ICS-LABA over-treats mild-persistent asthma; stepwise escalation begins with low-dose AIR therapy (Australian Asthma Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 2 weeks then taper with continued salbutamol PRN
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids are reserved for acute exacerbations or severe poorly controlled asthma; chronic oral steroids are inappropriate when inhaled options have not been trialled (Australian Asthma Handbook; AMH).
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Australian Asthma Handbook 2024 abandons SABA-only treatment in adults. The preferred reliever at all steps is low-dose ICS-formoterol (anti-inflammatory reliever, AIR). At higher severity it becomes maintenance and reliever therapy (MART). This reduces severe exacerbations and oral steroid bursts compared with SABA-only or daily ICS plus SABA reliever.
key_points: Adult asthma: no SABA-only at any step
Step 1-2: low-dose budesonide/formoterol PRN (AIR)
Step 3: low-dose budesonide/formoterol maintenance + reliever (MART)
Step 4: medium-dose MART
Step 5: high-dose ICS-LABA + add-on (LAMA, biologic) + specialist review
explanation.pearls: Reach for the brown puffer first, not the blue one - that's the headline shift in modern Australian asthma management.

sources.label: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

stem:
A 78-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressively worsening dyspnoea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. She had a right total knee replacement 4 weeks ago with delayed mobilisation. She has hypertension on amlodipine, osteoarthritis, and no prior VTE. She is on no anticoagulation since stopping enoxaparin 1 week post-op. She has had no haemoptysis but her right calf is mildly swollen with 2 cm difference compared with the left.

On arrival she is haemodynamically stable, SpO2 92 percent RA improving to 96 percent on 2 L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 102 bpm with no S1Q3T3 and no right heart strain pattern. CXR is unremarkable. D-dimer is 720 microg/L (laboratory standard cut-off 500 microg/L; age-adjusted cut-off age x 10 microg/L for age greater than 50).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 92% RA improving to 96% on 2 L NP, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Right calf swollen with 2 cm circumference difference, chest clear, no JVP elevation, S1 S2 no S3.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 102 bpm, no S1Q3T3. CXR: unremarkable. D-dimer 720 microg/L. Troponin pending. Creatinine 84 micromol/L.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Based on Wells score and D-dimer interpretation, which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home because the D-dimer sits below the age-adjusted threshold of 780 microg/L and therefore excludes the diagnosis
options.rationale: Age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 in patients >=50) is only valid in LOW pretest probability (Wells <=4, or 'PE unlikely'). Her Wells is 7.5 ('PE likely'), so D-dimer cannot be used as rule-out regardless of threshold. The anti-pattern is applying D-dimer to high-probability patients. Age-adjusted threshold is correct only in PE-unlikely patients (THANZ; BTS).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Order CT pulmonary angiogram and commence empirical therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting imaging
options.rationale: Her Wells score is high (greater than 4, 'PE likely'); D-dimer should not be used as a rule-out and CTPA is the first-line imaging. Empirical anticoagulation (LMWH or DOAC) is recommended while awaiting imaging if it is delayed beyond a few hours and bleeding risk is acceptable (eTG; THANZ; BTS).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Order V/Q scan as first-line imaging given the normal CXR
options.rationale: V/Q is correct when CTPA is contraindicated (severe contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy where V/Q may be preferred). With normal renal function and no allergy, CTPA is first-line. V/Q would be the correct first choice only with contrast contraindication or in pregnancy with normal CXR (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Repeat D-dimer in 24 hours and arrange outpatient CTPA if it rises
options.rationale: Delaying imaging in a high-probability patient is unsafe; PE mortality is concentrated in the first 24 hours. The anti-pattern is treating D-dimer as a screening test independent of pretest probability. Repeat D-dimer is essentially never correct in suspected acute PE (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Arrange bilateral lower-limb compression ultrasound first and only proceed to CTPA if positive
options.rationale: Lower-limb US is useful when chest imaging is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy with negative initial workup) or to add evidence in equivocal cases. It is not first-line when PE is the principal clinical concern with high pretest probability; a positive US confirms VTE but a negative US does not exclude PE (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

explanation.summary: Wells score for PE risk-stratifies into 'PE unlikely' (less than or equal to 4) and 'PE likely' (greater than 4). In 'PE unlikely', age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 microg/L if greater than 50) safely excludes PE if below threshold. In 'PE likely', proceed directly to CTPA; D-dimer is not applicable. Empirical anticoagulation while awaiting imaging is recommended if delay is expected and bleeding risk is acceptable.
key_points: Wells PE score: DVT signs 3, PE most likely dx 3, HR greater than 100 1.5, immobilisation/surgery 1.5, prior VTE 1.5, haemoptysis 1, malignancy 1
Wells greater than 4: PE likely - go to CTPA
Wells less than or equal to 4: PE unlikely - use D-dimer (age-adjusted if greater than 50)
V/Q if CTPA contraindicated
Empirical anticoagulation while awaiting CTPA if delay and acceptable bleeding risk
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer is only valid in 'PE unlikely' - using it in a high-probability patient gives false reassurance.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism - Wells score and age-adjusted D-dimer

stem:
A 52-year-old man is diagnosed with acute segmental pulmonary embolism on CTPA, performed for pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea after a long-haul flight from London 5 days ago. He has no prior VTE, no malignancy, and no recent surgery. On arrival he is haemodynamically stable, ambulating, eating, and drinking. His vital signs are stable as below. His troponin I and NT-proBNP are normal, and the CTPA reports no right heart strain.

He has stable home circumstances, lives 10 minutes from the hospital, and has a partner at home. He is not pregnant. He has no significant bleeding history and is not on antiplatelets or NSAIDs. His haemoglobin is 142 g/L, platelets 230 x 10^9/L, and creatinine 78 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest, chest clear, calves soft, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: right segmental PE, no right heart strain. Troponin I normal. NT-proBNP normal. Hb 142 g/L, platelets 230, creatinine 78.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Outpatient management with apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months
options.rationale: sPESI score of 0 (no malignancy, no chronic cardiopulmonary disease, age less than 80, HR less than 110, SBP greater than or equal to 100, SpO2 greater than or equal to 90 percent) indicates low-risk PE suitable for outpatient management with a DOAC; apixaban regimen is 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD for at least 3 months (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Inpatient management on a therapeutic enoxaparin bridge to warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 for at least 3 months of continued anticoagulation
options.rationale: Warfarin is no longer first-line for unprovoked PE without contraindications to DOACs; DOAC monotherapy avoids parenteral bridging and INR monitoring. Warfarin remains correct for antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive), severe renal impairment, mechanical valves, or where DOACs are unavailable/contraindicated (THANZ; eTG).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours followed by therapeutic heparin infusion and admission to a coronary care monitored bed
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (massive) PE with haemodynamic instability (sustained hypotension, shock) or selected intermediate-high-risk with deterioration. He is haemodynamically stable with no RV strain. Thrombolysis would only be correct with SBP <90 sustained, cardiac arrest, or progressive RV failure on therapeutic anticoagulation (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Inferior vena cava filter insertion without therapeutic anticoagulation given the recent long-haul flight as a transient provoking factor
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Recent long-haul flight is a transient provoking factor that justifies anticoagulation for 3 months but is not a contraindication. IVC filter would be correct only with active major bleeding precluding anticoagulation (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely without therapeutic anticoagulation given the segmental clot burden and absence of right heart strain
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is inadequate for acute PE treatment; therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 months is mandatory. Aspirin has a role in extended secondary prevention AFTER initial 6-12 months of therapeutic anticoagulation in low-recurrence-risk patients (ASPIRE/WARFASA trials), not as initial treatment (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

explanation.summary: Risk stratification of acute PE uses haemodynamic status, sPESI, RV dysfunction (echo or CT), and cardiac biomarkers. Low-risk PE (sPESI 0, no RV strain, normal biomarkers) can be managed as an outpatient with DOAC monotherapy. Intermediate and high-risk PE require admission, and high-risk (shock) PE may need thrombolysis.
key_points: sPESI: age greater than 80, malignancy, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR greater than or equal to 110, SBP less than 100, SpO2 less than 90 percent
sPESI 0 = low risk, suitable for outpatient management
DOAC monotherapy first-line: apixaban or rivaroxaban (no bridging)
Apixaban 10 mg BD x 7 days then 5 mg BD
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD x 21 days then 20 mg daily
Minimum 3 months anticoagulation; consider extended therapy if unprovoked
explanation.pearls: A long-haul flight makes the PE provoked, which typically caps anticoagulation duration at 3 months once the risk factor has resolved.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to ED with 3 days of fever, productive cough with rusty sputum, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea. He has a 25 pack-year smoking history, hypertension on perindopril, and no known drug allergies. On arrival he is alert but unwell-looking. His CXR shows dense right middle lobe consolidation with a small parapneumonic effusion. Bloods show WCC 18.4 x 10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 280 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, urea 9.2 mmol/L, glucose 7.8 mmol/L. ABG on room air shows pH 7.42, pO2 58 mmHg, pCO2 36 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/64 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 90% RA, T 38.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Alert, dehydrated, dullness and bronchial breathing right lower zone, no neck stiffness, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: dense right middle lobe consolidation with small effusion. WCC 18.4, CRP 280, albumin 28 g/L, creatinine 96, urea 9.2, glucose 7.8. ABG: pH 7.42, pO2 58, pCO2 36, HCO3 24.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate disposition and initial empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Admit to general ward today with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for atypical cover
options.rationale: His SMART-COP is high (multilobar + RR + oxygenation + albumin + SBP scores >=5), indicating high risk of needing intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Oral therapy and general ward miss this. The anti-pattern is anchoring on CURB-65 (which can underestimate in younger patients). Oral amoxicillin + doxycycline is correct for low-severity CAP (SMART-COP 0-2, CURB-65 0-1) (eTG Respiratory).

options.text: Admit to high-dependency or ICU; IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV azithromycin 500 mg daily, with empirical cover for atypicals
options.rationale: SMART-COP greater than or equal to 5 indicates a high risk of needing intensive respiratory or vasopressor support and warrants HDU/ICU-level care. Empirical therapy for severe CAP in Australia is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory).

options.text: Discharge home with a 7-day course of oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily based on a CURB-65 of only 1 today
options.rationale: Even if CURB-65 is reassuring at 1, his hypotension, hypoxia, multilobar disease, and biochemical derangements meet inpatient criteria. SMART-COP is more sensitive for need for intensive support in younger patients. Outpatient moxifloxacin would be correct only for low-severity CAP without inpatient indications (eTG Respiratory).

options.text: Admit to general ward today with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g six-hourly monotherapy and review at 48 hours for response to therapy
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not cover Mycoplasma, Legionella, or atypicals and is inadequate for severe CAP requiring ICU-level support. Benzylpenicillin can be used in confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia without atypical concern, but not as empirical therapy for severe CAP (eTG Respiratory).

options.text: Admit to ICU today with intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g twelve-hourly plus intravenous meropenem 1 g eight-hourly for empirical broad-spectrum coverage
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum antipseudomonal + MRSA cover is reserved for risk factors: structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis), recent hospitalisation, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, MRSA colonisation, or aspiration with structural disease. He has none of these. This combination would only be correct with documented risk factors or culture-directed therapy (eTG Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Australian severity scoring for CAP uses SMART-COP (intensive-support prediction) alongside CURB-65 (mortality prediction). SMART-COP greater than or equal to 5 indicates high risk of needing inotropic or respiratory support, warranting HDU/ICU. Severe CAP empirical therapy in Australia is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (or doxycycline) to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae plus atypicals.
key_points: SMART-COP: S BP less than 90 (2), M ultilobar (1), A lbumin less than 35 (1), R R greater than or equal to 25 (greater than or equal to 50 yo) (1), T achycardia greater than or equal to 125 (1), C onfusion (1), O xygen low (2), P H less than 7.35 (2)
SMART-COP greater than or equal to 5 = high risk of intensive support
CURB-65: Confusion, Urea greater than 7, RR greater than or equal to 30, BP less than 90 sys or less than or equal to 60 dia, age greater than or equal to 65
Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone + IV azithromycin (or doxycycline)
Step down to oral after 48 hours of clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP outperforms CURB-65 for predicting ICU need in younger patients - use both.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia - SMART-COP severity and antibiotic choice

stem:
An 82-year-old nursing home resident with advanced Parkinson disease and known dysphagia is brought to ED with 24 hours of fever, productive cough, and confusion. The nursing home reports she was found coughing during dinner the previous evening. She was hospitalised 3 weeks ago for a urinary tract infection and received IV ceftriaxone and oral ciprofloxacin during that admission. She has no documented multi-drug-resistant organism.

On examination she is febrile and tachypnoeic with right lower zone crackles. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. Bloods show neutrophilic leukocytosis and creatinine 96 micromol/L. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 2 L NP, T 38.4 degC, GCS 14.
data_table.Examination: Right lower zone crackles and dullness, no neck stiffness, mild dehydration.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe consolidation. WCC 14.6 x 10^9/L. CRP 180 mg/L. Creatinine 96 micromol/L.
data_table.Medications: Levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 mg QID, no antibiotics in past 6 months.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g eight-hourly empirically without antipseudomonal cover
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the standard empirical choice for community-onset aspiration pneumonia without risk factors, but her recent hospitalisation and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure within 90 days place her in the higher-risk category requiring broader empirical cover (eTG Respiratory).

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g six-hourly empirically with daily microbiology review
options.rationale: Recent hospitalisation plus recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure are eTG-listed risk factors for Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas in aspiration pneumonia; broader empirical cover with piperacillin-tazobactam is recommended pending cultures, with de-escalation once organism known (eTG Respiratory; Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily as monotherapy without anaerobic cover
options.rationale: Amoxicillin alone lacks beta-lactamase coverage for oral anaerobes and Gram-negatives, and oral therapy is inappropriate in this severity with hypoxia and confusion (eTG Respiratory).

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV metronidazole 500 mg twelve-hourly empirically
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone-metronidazole does not cover Pseudomonas and is less appropriate given her recent ceftriaxone exposure; routine metronidazole is no longer recommended by eTG even when amoxicillin-clavulanate is used (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

options.text: IV vancomycin 1.5 g twelve-hourly plus IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg twelve-hourly empirically
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus ciprofloxacin lacks adequate anaerobic cover and empirical vancomycin is not indicated without MRSA risk factors; recent fluoroquinolone exposure also makes empirical ciprofloxacin a poor choice (eTG Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Aspiration pneumonia empirical therapy in Australian guidelines is amoxicillin-clavulanate (IV or oral depending on severity), which covers typical respiratory pathogens plus oral anaerobes. Routine addition of metronidazole is no longer recommended. Severity escalates to broader cover only with structural lung disease, recent hospitalisation, or prior MDRO. Address modifiable risk factors: dysphagia management, oral care, head-of-bed elevation, medication review for sedatives.
key_points: Empirical: amoxicillin-clavulanate (IV 1.2 g 8-hourly, oral 875+125 mg BD)
Routine metronidazole addition no longer recommended
Broaden if recent hospitalisation, structural lung disease, MDRO risk
Address dysphagia, oral hygiene, sedative review
Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical) does not need antibiotics unless secondary infection
explanation.pearls: Distinguish aspiration pneumonitis (acute chemical injury, no antibiotics) from aspiration pneumonia (clinical infection, antibiotics) - the time course matters.

subtopic_detail: Aspiration pneumonia - antibiotic choice and risk factors

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to ED with palpitations and mild dyspnoea that began approximately 32 hours ago, but he reports a similar but milder episode 4 days ago that he ignored. He has hypertension on perindopril and no other medical history. He is haemodynamically stable. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation at 102 bpm. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows preserved LV function (LVEF 60 percent), mild left atrial dilatation (LA 42 mm), and no significant valvular disease.

He has no prior stroke, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, or heart failure, and has never been anticoagulated. CHA2DS2-VA score is 1 (hypertension). The team would like to attempt rhythm control on this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 102 bpm irregular, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, chest clear, no neurological deficit, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF rate 102. Echo: LVEF 60 percent, LA 42 mm, no valve disease. TSH normal, K 4.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate approach to cardioversion?

options.text: Proceed to electrical cardioversion now without anticoagulation since current episode is under 48 hours
options.rationale: The 48-hour window applies only when AF onset is genuinely certain; his earlier symptomatic episode 4 days ago makes total duration uncertain, mandating either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or a TOE before cardioversion (CSANZ/NHFA AF 2018).

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation and perform TOE-guided cardioversion, then continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks regardless of CHA2DS2-VA
options.rationale: When AF onset is uncertain or greater than 48 hours, CSANZ requires either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or TOE-guided cardioversion; anticoagulation must continue for at least 4 weeks post-cardioversion due to atrial stunning, independent of CHA2DS2-VA score, which only governs longer-term anticoagulation.

options.text: Commence aspirin 100 mg daily and proceed to elective electrical cardioversion in 24 hours
options.rationale: Aspirin provides no useful stroke protection peri-cardioversion; therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin, LMWH, DOAC, or warfarin is required (CSANZ/NHFA AF 2018).

options.text: Defer cardioversion indefinitely and use rate control with metoprolol without anticoagulation
options.rationale: Indefinite deferral of rhythm control loses the symptomatic benefit of restoring sinus rhythm in a first symptomatic episode (EAST-AFNET 4); rate control alone does not exempt from anticoagulation decisions guided by CHA2DS2-VA.

options.text: Discharge home, commence flecainide pill-in-pocket strategy and review in clinic next week
