sources.label: HSANZ position statement on sickle cell disease
BSH Sickle Cell Disease in Adults Guideline 2015

stem:
A 74-year-old woman attends ED with one day of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild exertional dyspnoea. She had a knee arthroplasty 8 weeks ago. She has hypertension on perindopril, osteoarthritis, no haemoptysis, no calf swelling, no malignancy and is otherwise active. Examination: comfortable at rest, clear chest, no calf signs, SpO2 96 percent on room air. ECG sinus tachycardia 102.

CXR normal. Bloods: troponin negative, FBC normal, eGFR 68. Wells score is 1.5 (recent surgery 1.5; PE most likely diagnosis criterion not counted). Age-adjusted D-dimer returns at 680 microgram/L FEU.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.7 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Clear chest, no calf signs, comfortable at rest.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative, ECG sinus tachycardia, CXR normal, eGFR 68, FBC normal, Wells score 1.5 (PE unlikely).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Exclude PE based on Wells unlikely plus D-dimer 680 microgram/L below the age-adjusted cut-off of 740, and discharge with safety netting
options.rationale: In Wells PE-unlikely patients over 50, the age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off is age x 10 microgram/L FEU (740 here). A value of 680 lies below this cut-off and safely excludes PE per ADJUST-PE and eTG, sparing her CTPA contrast and radiation; safety netting and follow-up are appropriate.

options.text: Proceed to CTPA because the D-dimer is above the standard fixed cut-off of 500 microgram/L
options.rationale: Applying the fixed cut-off in patients over 50 over-investigates them; age-adjusted cut-off is the correct rule and avoids unnecessary CTPA (ADJUST-PE; eTG).

options.text: Start therapeutic anticoagulation empirically and image with CTPA within 24 hours
options.rationale: Empirical anticoagulation pending imaging is reserved for Wells-likely patients with delayed imaging, not Wells-unlikely with a negative age-adjusted D-dimer (eTG; BTS).

options.text: Perform V/Q scan as the first-line confirmatory test because CXR is normal
options.rationale: V/Q is preferred when contrast is contraindicated; in her case PE is already excluded by Wells-unlikely plus negative age-adjusted D-dimer (eTG).

options.text: Repeat D-dimer in 24 hours before deciding on imaging
options.rationale: Repeating D-dimer adds no diagnostic information when the original is already below the age-adjusted cut-off; PE is excluded (eTG).

explanation.summary: In Wells PE-unlikely patients (score <= 4), age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 micrograms/L FEU for those over 50) safely excludes PE without CTPA. A negative result has high NPV; if positive, proceed to imaging (eTG; ADJUST-PE).
key_points: Wells <= 4 = PE unlikely; use D-dimer
Age-adjusted cut-off (age x 10) above age 50
Wells > 4 = PE likely; go to CTPA directly
V/Q reserved for contrast contraindications
explanation.pearls: The Wells 'PE most likely diagnosis' criterion is 3 points and the most subjective - apply judiciously.

stem:
A 67-year-old man with newly diagnosed metastatic colorectal cancer (liver metastases) presents with a confirmed unprovoked left iliofemoral DVT and segmental subsegmental PE on CTPA. He started FOLFOX chemotherapy 10 days ago. He is haemodynamically stable, normotensive and not hypoxic. He has chronic kidney disease with eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2, no liver dysfunction (bilirubin 16, ALT 28), and no prior GI bleeding.

He has a colostomy after primary resection. There is no upper GI lesion documented on endoscopy 3 months ago. He has no thrombocytopenia (platelets 188) and no anaemia. He is not on antiplatelets. He has no history of intracranial haemorrhage. He weighs 78 kg. He is on ondansetron for nausea, dexamethasone PRN with chemotherapy, paracetamol for analgesia and atorvastatin 40 mg.

He is keen to take an oral agent and avoid daily injections if possible. He understands that anticoagulation must continue for at least the duration of active malignancy. He has no platelet transfusion history and no autoimmune disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: Left leg swelling to mid-thigh, palpable colostomy site, no jaundice.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 188, eGFR 38, bilirubin 16, ALT 28, INR 1.0, no upper GI lesion on endoscopy 3 months ago.
data_table.Medications: FOLFOX chemotherapy, ondansetron, dexamethasone PRN, paracetamol, atorvastatin 40 mg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation choice?

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg daily
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is acceptable for non-luminal cancer VTE but has higher GI bleed risk than apixaban in CAT trials (SELECT-D, CARAVAGGIO); the standard 20 mg dose also requires CrCl >50 mL/min. The anti-pattern is reflexive rivaroxaban for any DOAC indication. Rivaroxaban would be correct only if apixaban were unavailable and bleeding risk were low (eviQ; AMH).

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg BD after 5 days of LMWH lead-in
options.rationale: Dabigatran requires a 5-day parenteral LMWH lead-in (no immediate oral start) and is contraindicated when CrCl <30 with limited data at CrCl 30-50. Dabigatran was not studied as first-line in CAT trials and is not preferred. Dabigatran would be reasonable in non-cancer VTE with normal renal function (AMH; eviQ).

options.text: Warfarin bridged with LMWH until INR 2-3 stable
options.rationale: Warfarin is inferior to LMWH and DOACs in CAT due to drug-drug interactions with chemo, erratic INR control during nausea/vomiting, and lack of evidence for non-inferiority. Warfarin is correct only when DOACs and LMWH cannot be used (mechanical valve, severe renal impairment, prior DOAC failure) (eviQ).

options.text: Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD
options.rationale: In cancer-associated thrombosis without luminal GI malignancy and with eGFR over 30, apixaban (preferred for renal impairment among DOACs) or LMWH are first-line; apixaban has the lowest GI bleed signal of DOACs and meets the patient's oral-preference goal (eviQ Cancer-associated thrombosis; eTG).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily as secondary prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin is NOT acceptable monotherapy for acute VTE. It is considered only for extended secondary prevention AFTER 3-6 months of full anticoagulation in selected non-cancer low-recurrence patients (ASPIRE/WARFASA). Aspirin alone is essentially never correct for acute CAT (eTG).

explanation.summary: For cancer-associated thrombosis without luminal GI or GU malignancy, apixaban or LMWH are first-line. Apixaban has the lowest bleeding signal of DOACs and is preferred when eGFR is 30-49 (eviQ; eTG).
key_points: Luminal GI/GU cancer = caution with DOACs; consider LMWH
Apixaban dose: 10 mg BD x 7 days then 5 mg BD
Continue anticoagulation while cancer active
Avoid dabigatran when CrCl is borderline
explanation.pearls: CAT recurrence is highest in the first 3 months - don't switch agents prematurely.

stem:
A 72-year-old man is on day 8 post coronary artery bypass grafting. He has been on prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily since day 1 plus an intraoperative and 48-hour post-op unfractionated heparin infusion. He develops a new right calf DVT confirmed on ultrasound. Platelets have fallen from 280 to 78 (a 72 percent drop). No bleeding, no skin necrosis, no schistocytes on film.

PF4-heparin ELISA is strongly positive and a serotonin release assay is pending. 4Ts score is 7. He has CKD with eGFR 38 (creatinine 168 micromol/L) and severe hepatic dysfunction from chronic right heart failure (bilirubin 62, INR 1.6).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 37.0 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Right calf swollen and tender, no skin necrosis, no bleeding, sternotomy wound clean.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (pre-op 280), Hb 102 g/L, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, no schistocytes, PF4 antibody strongly positive ELISA, 4Ts 7 (high probability), eGFR 42.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate anticoagulation strategy?

options.text: Stop all heparin (UFH and LMWH) and commence IV bivalirudin at adjusted dose given combined renal and hepatic impairment, with close aPTT monitoring
options.rationale: HIT requires stopping all heparins and starting a non-heparin therapeutic anticoagulant. Argatroban is preferred in renal impairment but contraindicated in significant hepatic dysfunction (predominantly hepatic clearance), and fondaparinux is renally cleared and contraindicated at eGFR under 30. Bivalirudin has both renal and hepatic dose-adjustable clearance, making it the appropriate choice when both organs are impaired (ASH 2018; eTG).

options.text: Stop heparin and commence fondaparinux 7.5 mg SC daily off-label at standard dose
options.rationale: Fondaparinux is renally cleared and contraindicated at eGFR under 30; her eGFR of 38 sits in the dose-reduction zone but combined with hepatic dysfunction makes bivalirudin a safer choice (ASH 2018; AMH).

options.text: Stop heparin and commence IV argatroban at standard dose
options.rationale: Argatroban is hepatically cleared and contraindicated in significant hepatic dysfunction (bilirubin 62, INR 1.6); it would accumulate and over-anticoagulate (ASH 2018; AMH).

options.text: Stop heparin and immediately commence warfarin bridging to therapeutic INR 2.0 to 3.0
options.rationale: Warfarin must not be started in acute HIT until platelets recover above 150, due to risk of warfarin-induced skin necrosis from protein C depletion (ASH 2018).

options.text: Stop all heparin and observe expectantly without alternative anticoagulation until platelets recover
options.rationale: HIT is prothrombotic; stopping heparin without substitute therapeutic anticoagulation leaves him at high risk of further venous and arterial events (ASH 2018).

explanation.summary: HIT is a clinical-laboratory diagnosis with a high 4Ts score plus a positive PF4 antibody confirmed by functional assay. Stop all heparin (UFH and LMWH) AND substitute a non-heparin therapeutic anticoagulant; do not give warfarin or platelets in acute phase (ASH 2018).
key_points: 4Ts 0-3 low, 4-5 intermediate, 6-8 high probability
Stop all heparin AND substitute therapeutic non-heparin agent
Avoid warfarin in acute HIT until platelets > 150
Avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion
explanation.pearls: Timing nadir 5-10 days post heparin exposure is classic; rapid-onset HIT (<24 hours) occurs with recent prior exposure within 100 days.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with one week of mucocutaneous bruising, gum bleeding, two short epistaxis episodes, and today new heavy menstrual bleeding requiring an overnight pad change every 90 minutes. She takes no medications, has not been recently vaccinated, has no recent viral illness, no pregnancy. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Bloods: isolated platelets 4 x10^9/L with normal Hb, WCC, differential, coagulation profile, renal and liver function. Blood film: large platelets, no schistocytes, no blasts. HIV, hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, ANA all negative. The team plans urgent treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, T 36.6 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Petechiae lower limbs and buccal mucosa, bruising, gingival oozing, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 8 x10^9/L, Hb 132, WCC 6.4 normal differential, INR 1.0, APTT 30, blood film large platelets no blasts, HIV/HBV/HCV negative, ANA negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days plus IVIG 1 g/kg as combination first-line therapy
options.rationale: Severe ITP (platelets under 20 with active bleeding requiring intervention) is treated with combination corticosteroid plus IVIG for rapid platelet rise, per ASH 2019 and eTG; IVIG raises platelets within 24 to 48 hours, while corticosteroid (oral or pulsed IV) provides sustained immunomodulation. Heavy menstrual bleeding with platelets of 4 is bleeding sufficient to warrant combination, not monotherapy (ASH 2019; eTG Haematology).

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily as monotherapy and review platelet count in 1 week
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy takes days to weeks to raise platelets; with active heavy bleeding and platelets of 4, the more rapid combined IVIG plus steroid response is preferred (ASH 2019).

options.text: Platelet transfusion of 2 adult therapeutic doses to correct count above 50 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Transfused platelets are rapidly consumed by the same autoantibody and rarely raise count meaningfully in stable ITP; transfusion is reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage (intracranial, major GI) alongside other therapies (ASH 2019; ANZSBT).
source_refs: ANZSBT Guidelines for the Administration of Blood Products

options.text: Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 weekly for 4 weeks as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Rituximab is second-line for steroid-refractory or relapsing ITP, not first-line (ASH 2019).

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy first to confirm the diagnosis before commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Bone marrow biopsy is not required in typical adult ITP with isolated thrombocytopenia and normal film; treatment must not be delayed when bleeding is active (ASH 2019).

explanation.summary: Adult ITP first-line is corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg or short dexamethasone pulse). IVIG is added when more rapid platelet rise is needed (active bleeding, procedure imminent). Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleeding (ASH 2019).
key_points: First-line: corticosteroids
Add IVIG 1 g/kg if rapid response needed
Anti-D in Rh-positive non-splenectomised patients - alternative
Treatment threshold: platelets <30 or bleeding
explanation.pearls: Avoid platelet transfusion in stable ITP - the antibodies eat them in hours.

sources.label: ANZSBT Guidelines for the Administration of Blood Products

subtopic_detail: Urgent FBC + blood film + bone marrow
stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to her GP with three weeks of progressive fatigue, easy bruising of the limbs, gum bleeding and a low-grade fever. She had two episodes of unexplained epistaxis lasting 15 minutes each. She has no past medical history of note and takes no medications. She has lost 3 kg unintentionally in the last month and has drenching night sweats.

She has no foreign travel and no contact with TB. On examination she is pale, with widespread bruising and petechiae, gum hypertrophy and bleeding, a 4 cm palpable spleen and shotty cervical lymphadenopathy. Bloods at her GP show pancytopenia: Hb 76 g/L, WCC 38 x10^9/L (with 70% blasts on differential), platelets 14 x10^9/L. Blood film reports myeloid blasts with Auer rods.

Coagulation profile shows fibrinogen 1.0 g/L (low) and a raised D-dimer. She has not received transfusion. She is haemodynamically stable but the GP is concerned about possible acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML). She has no current bleeding source other than gums.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 37.6 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Pale, widespread bruising and petechiae, gum hypertrophy and bleeding, 4 cm splenomegaly, shotty cervical nodes.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76 g/L, WCC 38 x10^9/L (70% blasts with Auer rods), platelets 14 x10^9/L, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L, D-dimer 6.5, LDH 980, urate 0.52 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with routine outpatient haematology referral in 2 weeks for further workup
options.rationale: Suspected APML with coagulopathy is a haematological emergency with very high early mortality (DIC-driven intracranial haemorrhage). Outpatient referral is unsafe and misses the time-critical window for ATRA. Outpatient haematology is correct only for stable chronic conditions, never with circulating blasts plus DIC (eviQ).

options.text: Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and observe in ED for 24 hours before specialist referral
options.rationale: Antibiotics may be needed if febrile neutropenia develops, but they must not delay urgent haematology transfer and empirical ATRA. The anti-pattern is treating one issue (potential sepsis) and missing the dominant threat (coagulopathy and early haemorrhagic death). Antibiotics are concurrent, not first (eviQ).

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells and 1 pool of platelets then reassess clinically
options.rationale: Transfusion support (FFP, cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen >1.5, platelets >50) may be appropriate but is not the SINGLE next step - definitive treatment (ATRA + bone marrow + transfer) is the priority. Aggressive transfusion is correct as adjunct to ATRA during the high-risk first 14 days (ANZSBT; eviQ).

options.text: Same-day transfer to haematology for urgent bone marrow biopsy with empirical ATRA if APML suspected
options.rationale: Acute leukaemia with coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer) and Auer rods on film highly suggests APML; empirical all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is started on clinical suspicion (do not wait for confirmation) because of bleeding-death risk. Urgent transfer for bone marrow, cytogenetics and PML-RARA testing (eviQ; BSH AML Guideline).

options.text: Repeat the full blood count in 48 hours to confirm the pancytopenia before any specialist referral
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts is diagnostic of leukaemia until proven otherwise; delay is unsafe especially with coagulopathy. The anti-pattern is treating any abnormal result as needing 'await trend' before specialist involvement. Repeat FBC is appropriate only for borderline cytopenia without blasts (eviQ).

explanation.summary: Acute leukaemia with Auer rods plus coagulopathy is APML until proven otherwise. Same-day transfer to a haematology centre and empirical ATRA initiation reduce early haemorrhagic death (eviQ; BSH AML Guideline).
key_points: Blasts + Auer rods + coagulopathy = APML
ATRA empirically on suspicion - do not wait for confirmation
Same-day haematology transfer
Aggressive blood product support during induction
explanation.pearls: APML is the most curable acute leukaemia but early death from coagulopathy is the killer - ATRA is started before cytogenetics confirm PML-RARA.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with stage A (Binet) CLL diagnosed 18 months ago has been on watch-and-wait. His lymphocyte count has been stable around 18-22 x10^9/L. He attends with three weeks of unilateral right cervical lymph node enlargement that is now 5 cm, firm and rapidly growing. He has lost 6 kg in the last month, has drenching night sweats and a temperature of 38.4 deg C this morning.

His Hb is 102 g/L (was 132), LDH is 920 U/L (was 220) and uric acid is 0.48 mmol/L. He has no infection elsewhere. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis shows bulky cervical, mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy with a dominant 5 x 4 cm right cervical node. PET-CT shows the dominant node has SUVmax 18 with significantly higher avidity than other nodes. He has not had previous chemotherapy. He has not received rituximab. His original CLL FISH showed del(13q) only. He has no concurrent infection on cultures.

data_table.Examination: 5 cm firm right cervical lymph node, generalised lymphadenopathy, 3 cm splenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (was 132), WCC 24 (lymphocytes 18), platelets 142, LDH 920 (was 220), uric acid 0.48, beta-2 microglobulin elevated, blood film smudge cells with some larger atypical cells, PET-CT dominant node SUVmax 18.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly suggests Richter transformation requiring biopsy?

options.text: Lymphocyte count rising from 18 to 22 x10^9/L over 18 months without lymphadenopathy or B symptoms
options.rationale: Slow lymphocyte rise is expected in untreated CLL and does NOT indicate transformation; doubling time matters more than absolute count (lymphocyte doubling <6 months is a treatment-indicating feature). The anti-pattern is interpreting any rise as transformation. Rapid rise (doubling <6 months) indicates active progression, but transformation requires biopsy evidence (BSH CLL Guideline).

options.text: Smudge cells on the blood film with no rising LDH, new lymphadenopathy or constitutional symptoms
options.rationale: Smudge cells (Gumprecht shadows) are characteristic of CLL itself - fragile lymphocytes ruptured during smear preparation. They are a diagnostic feature, not a transformation marker. Their absence/presence does not track disease evolution (BSH CLL).

options.text: PET avidity SUVmax >10 in a dominant node alongside rising LDH and B symptoms in a known CLL patient
options.rationale: Richter transformation (CLL evolving to aggressive lymphoma, usually diffuse large B-cell) is suggested by rapidly enlarging asymmetric nodes, B symptoms, marked LDH rise and PET SUVmax >10 in a dominant node. Biopsy of the most FDG-avid node is required for diagnosis (BSH CLL Guideline; eviQ).

options.text: Hb 102 g/L alone without rising LDH or any new lymphadenopathy on recent examination today
options.rationale: Mild anaemia can reflect marrow infiltration in progressive CLL without indicating transformation; Hb 102 in isolation could also be unrelated (concurrent IDA, ACD). Combined with other features it may support transformation, but in isolation it is non-specific. Anaemia is a Rai/Binet progression marker, not specifically Richter (BSH CLL).

options.text: Original FISH showing del(13q) as the sole cytogenetic abnormality at initial diagnosis years earlier
options.rationale: Isolated del(13q) is a FAVOURABLE prognostic marker in CLL with the best survival of all FISH subtypes; it does not predict Richter transformation. The anti-pattern is treating any cytogenetic finding as ominous. del(17p) and TP53 mutation carry higher transformation risk (BSH CLL).

explanation.summary: Richter transformation should be suspected in CLL patients with rapidly enlarging asymmetric nodes, B symptoms, sharply rising LDH and PET SUVmax >10 in a dominant node; excisional biopsy of the most FDG-avid node confirms diagnosis (BSH CLL Guideline).
key_points: Watch-and-wait: stable CLL without symptoms, cytopenias or bulk
Treatment triggers: B symptoms, progressive cytopenias, bulky/symptomatic nodes, doubling time <6 months
Richter transformation: ~5-10% lifetime risk
Biopsy most FDG-avid node
explanation.pearls: del(17p) and TP53 mutations predict Richter risk and require targeted agents (BTK/BCL2 inhibitors) rather than chemoimmunotherapy.

stem:
A 24-year-old previously well woman has been diagnosed with classical Hodgkin lymphoma after excisional left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy. Immunohistochemistry: CD30 positive, CD15 positive, CD20 negative Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. She reports drenching night sweats, fevers above 38, and 8 kg weight loss over 6 weeks. PET-CT shows supradiaphragmatic-only nodal involvement (left supraclavicular, mediastinal, bilateral cervical). Bloods: Hb 116, WCC normal, ESR 68, LDH normal, HIV negative.

Echocardiogram shows LVEF 60 percent. Pulmonary function tests are normal. She has not commenced any treatment yet. She has no children but wishes to preserve fertility.

data_table.Examination: 4 cm firm left supraclavicular lymph node, bilateral cervical nodes, mild splenomegaly, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: Excisional node biopsy: CD30+ CD15+ CD20- bi-nucleate Reed-Sternberg cells in mixed inflammatory infiltrate. PET-CT supradiaphragmatic only.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step before commencing chemotherapy?

options.text: Refer urgently for fertility preservation counselling and oocyte or embryo cryopreservation, then commence ABVD chemotherapy
options.rationale: ABVD chemotherapy (standard first-line for early-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma with B symptoms is generally early-unfavourable disease per Australian and European stratification) carries low to moderate gonadotoxicity but the cumulative effect with potential radiotherapy and BEACOPP for relapse means fertility preservation should be offered before treatment begins. eviQ and HSANZ explicitly recommend urgent fertility referral before chemotherapy in young patients (eviQ Hodgkin; HSANZ).

options.text: Commence ABVD chemotherapy immediately and defer fertility discussion until after first cycle
options.rationale: Delaying fertility discussion until after chemotherapy starts misses the window for oocyte or embryo cryopreservation (which requires ovarian stimulation pre-treatment); fertility referral must occur before first cycle (eviQ).

options.text: Commence BEACOPP chemotherapy as first-line for B symptoms instead of ABVD
options.rationale: ABVD is standard first-line in Australia for classical Hodgkin lymphoma; BEACOPP is reserved for advanced-stage disease or relapse, with greater gonadotoxicity (eviQ; HSANZ).

options.text: Proceed directly to involved-site radiotherapy as monotherapy without chemotherapy
options.rationale: Combined modality (chemotherapy plus radiotherapy in selected cases) is standard; radiotherapy monotherapy is not used for HL with B symptoms (eviQ).

options.text: Repeat excisional lymph node biopsy to confirm the immunohistochemistry findings before treatment
options.rationale: Diagnosis is already established with CD30 positive CD15 positive CD20 negative Reed-Sternberg cells; repeat biopsy is not required and delays treatment (eviQ).

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma rests on Reed-Sternberg cells with the CD30+ CD15+ CD20- immunophenotype in a mixed inflammatory background; clinical features (alcohol-induced pain, contiguous spread) are supportive but not diagnostic (BSH Hodgkin; eviQ).
key_points: Reed-Sternberg = Hodgkin (classical)
CD30+ CD15+ CD20- in classical Hodgkin
B symptoms not discriminating between HL and NHL
Stage by Ann Arbor; A/B for absence/presence of B symptoms
explanation.pearls: Bimodal age distribution (15-35 and >50) is characteristic of Hodgkin.

stem: A 70-year-old man is being evaluated for symptomatic multiple myeloma. He has back pain (mid-thoracic, worse at night), 4 kg unintentional weight loss, two recent pneumonias, T6 spinal tenderness without neurological deficit. Bloods: Hb 92 g/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (eGFR 28; baseline 78), corrected calcium 2.78 mmol/L (RR 2.10 to 2.60), albumin 28, IgG kappa paraprotein 42 g/L, kappa free light chain 320 mg/L (ratio 28), urinary Bence Jones protein positive. CT shows multiple lytic lesions and a T6 compression fracture. Bone marrow biopsy: 45 percent clonal plasma cells.

data_table.Examination: T6 spinal tenderness, no neurological deficit, no peripheral neuropathy.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (eGFR 28), corrected Ca 2.78, albumin 28, IgG kappa paraprotein 42 g/L, FLC kappa 320 mg/L (ratio 28), urinary BJP positive, lytic lesions on CT, compression fx at T6.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combination of next steps in management?

options.text: Urgent MRI whole spine for cord compression risk, IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid, IV zoledronic acid (dose-adjusted for renal function), and refer to haematology to commence bortezomib-based induction
options.rationale: He meets CRAB criteria with active myeloma. The T6 compression fracture in painful spine mandates urgent MRI to exclude cord compression. Hypercalcaemia requires IV hydration and bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid is the standard, with dose adjustment at eGFR 28 per AMH); bortezomib-based induction (e.g. VTd or VRd) is preferred over lenalidomide-based regimens in significant renal impairment (eviQ Myeloma; HSANZ; eTG).
source_refs: HSANZ position statement on multiple myeloma

options.text: Repeat bone marrow biopsy and skeletal survey for staging before commencing any myeloma-directed therapy, with analgesia and oral hydration in the interim and outpatient haematology review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Bone marrow (45 percent plasma cells) and CT skeletal imaging are already done; further delay risks cord compression and worsening renal failure (eviQ).

options.text: Commence high-dose dexamethasone 40 mg daily as monotherapy induction, arrange oral hydration at home, and discharge with outpatient haematology and renal follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Dexamethasone alone is inadequate induction and discharge with painful compression fracture and severe AKI is unsafe; multidisciplinary inpatient management is required (eviQ).

options.text: Commence high-dose lenalidomide-based induction immediately at standard dose, with IV hydration and analgesia, and arrange MRI spine and inpatient haematology review during the admission
options.rationale: Lenalidomide requires substantial dose reduction at eGFR under 30 and bortezomib-based regimens are preferred in significant renal impairment due to faster reduction of paraprotein and better renal recovery (eviQ; AMH).

options.text: Commence emergency haemodialysis as the primary intervention to clear paraprotein, give IV zoledronic acid for hypercalcaemia, and defer all chemotherapy until renal function recovers to baseline
options.rationale: Dialysis does not effectively clear intact paraprotein; renal recovery in myeloma is driven by reducing light chain production via systemic therapy (bortezomib-based), with dialysis reserved for life-threatening uraemia or fluid overload (eviQ).

explanation.summary: CRAB criteria define active myeloma: hyperCalcaemia >2.75, Renal impairment (Cr >177 or CrCl <40), Anaemia (Hb <100), Bone lesions. The 2014 update added SLiM criteria: clonal plasma cells >=60%, FLC ratio >=100, >1 focal lesion on MRI. Paraprotein size separates MGUS from smouldering myeloma but is not CRAB (IMWG).
key_points: CRAB = Calcium, Renal, Anaemia, Bone
SLiM = >=60% plasma cells, FLC ratio >=100, >1 MRI focal lesion
MGUS = paraprotein <30, no CRAB, plasma cells <10%
Smouldering = paraprotein >=30 OR plasma cells 10-60%, no CRAB
explanation.pearls: Back pain + anaemia + raised Ca + raised creatinine in an older adult = myeloma until proven otherwise.

sources.label: HSANZ position statement on multiple myeloma
IMWG Diagnostic Criteria for Multiple Myeloma

stem:
A 38-year-old man is admitted with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma with extensive abdominal disease, bulky retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and bone marrow involvement. He is haemodynamically stable. Pre-chemotherapy bloods show urate 0.62 mmol/L (RR 0.20-0.42), potassium 4.6, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, calcium 2.30, creatinine 92 (eGFR 86), LDH 4800 U/L (>10x upper limit), WCC 14 with 8% blasts on film. He has no known G6PD deficiency but has not been formally tested.

He is not pregnant. He is to start intensive R-CODOX-M/IVAC chemotherapy within 24 hours. He has no significant cardiac history. He is in a tertiary haematology unit with continuous monitoring. He has good IV access. He has no allopurinol allergy. The haematology team classifies him as high risk for tumour lysis syndrome by Cairo-Bishop criteria. The unit has rasburicase available. Renal output is currently 80 mL/hr. He weighs 75 kg.

data_table.Examination: Bulky abdominal mass, otherwise well.
data_table.Investigations: Urate 0.62 mmol/L, K 4.6, phosphate 1.6, corrected Ca 2.30, creatinine 92, LDH 4800, WCC 14 with 8% blasts.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic strategy for tumour lysis syndrome in this high-risk patient?

options.text: Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV daily plus IV hydration 3 L/m^2/day with close electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: High-risk TLS (Burkitt, raised baseline urate, LDH >10x ULN) is managed with rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) which actively breaks down existing urate, generous IV hydration to maintain urine output >100 mL/m^2/hr and 6-8 hourly electrolyte monitoring during the first 72 hours. Screen for G6PD deficiency first - rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (BSH TLS; eviQ).

options.text: Allopurinol 300 mg daily and IV fluid hydration 2 L/m^2/day, without any rasburicase use
options.rationale: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase to prevent NEW urate formation but does NOT clear existing urate. Adequate for intermediate-risk TLS (lower LDH, less bulky disease). The anti-pattern is using allopurinol in true high-risk TLS where pre-existing urate is already very high. Allopurinol is correct for intermediate-risk only (Cairo-Bishop; BSH TLS Guideline; eviQ).

options.text: Urinary alkalinisation with intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion targeting urine pH above 7.5 consistently
options.rationale: Routine urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended; it increases calcium phosphate precipitation in tubules (which is less soluble at higher pH) and offers no benefit when rasburicase is used. The anti-pattern is using an obsolete strategy from the pre-rasburicase era. Alkalinisation is correct only if rasburicase is unavailable AND allopurinol is being used (BSH TLS).

options.text: Delay chemotherapy by 7 days to allow oral allopurinol to reduce baseline serum urate substantially
options.rationale: Burkitt lymphoma has a doubling time of 24-48 hours; delaying chemotherapy by 7 days for prophylactic urate lowering is inappropriate and risks rapid clinical deterioration. Rasburicase normalises urate within hours, eliminating the need to delay. Delay would be correct only in very low-grade malignancy with TLS risk (essentially never) (eviQ).

options.text: Prophylactic upfront haemodialysis arranged via nephrology prior to commencing the first chemotherapy cycle
options.rationale: Prophylactic dialysis is reserved for established TLS with refractory hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, or oliguria; pre-emptive dialysis is not standard prophylaxis. Dialysis is correct for severe established TLS with AKI requiring renal replacement, not as primary prevention (BSH TLS).

explanation.summary: High-risk TLS (Burkitt, ALL with WCC >100, raised baseline urate, LDH >10x ULN) requires rasburicase plus generous IV hydration plus 6-8 hourly electrolyte monitoring. Screen for G6PD before rasburicase. Allopurinol is for intermediate risk (BSH TLS; eviQ).
key_points: Cairo-Bishop laboratory TLS: 2+ of urate, K, phosphate, Ca derangements
High risk: Burkitt, ALL WCC >100, bulky LDH >10x ULN
Rasburicase: clears existing urate (not allopurinol)
Avoid rasburicase in G6PD deficiency
explanation.pearls: Routine alkalinisation is OUT - increases calcium phosphate crystallisation.

stem:
A 54-year-old woman with AML on day 12 of induction chemotherapy presents to the haematology ward with a temperature of 38.5 deg C on two readings 30 minutes apart. She has had mild rigors. She has no localising symptoms. Her central venous catheter exit site is clean. Her oral mucosa shows grade 2 mucositis without obvious infection. Her last chemotherapy was cytarabine plus daunorubicin completed 8 days ago.

She has no penicillin allergy. She has been on aciclovir and fluconazole prophylaxis. She has had no recent travel. She is haemodynamically stable. Her current bloods show neutrophil count 0.2 x10^9/L (severe neutropenia), Hb 92, platelets 38, creatinine 72, lactate 1.4, CRP 78. Blood cultures from the line and a peripheral site are drawn before any antibiotic is given. CXR is clear.

Urine dipstick is negative. There is no diarrhoea or cough. She has good IV access. Her MASCC score is calculated as 18 (lower risk, but with mucositis). She has had no antibiotics in the last 90 days. She has no recent C. difficile.

data_table.Examination: Grade 2 oral mucositis, clean CVC exit site, no rash, no focal signs.
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.2 x10^9/L, Hb 92, platelets 38, creatinine 72, lactate 1.4, CRP 78, CXR clear, blood cultures sent.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin home outpatient regimen
options.rationale: Outpatient oral regimens are restricted to selected low-risk MASCC >=21 patients without mucositis or profound/prolonged neutropenia and with reliable follow-up. This patient with grade 2 mucositis and neutrophils 0.2 is not eligible. Outpatient oral therapy is correct for MASCC >=21 with no mucositis and stable observation arrangements (eTG; eviQ).

options.text: Meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours as first-line
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for second-line in persistent fever after 72-96 hours on first-line, septic shock, or known ESBL/AmpC carriage - not first-line empirical therapy. The anti-pattern is broad-spectrum-first stewardship failure. Meropenem is correct after first-line failure, septic shock, or documented resistant organism (eTG).

options.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus caspofungin from the outset
options.rationale: Empirical vancomycin is not added routinely from the outset; reserved for suspected line infection, skin/soft tissue infection, haemodynamic instability, or MRSA colonisation. Empirical antifungal is added if fever persists beyond 72-96 hours despite broad antibacterials. Triple therapy from outset is over-treatment with toxicity. This combination is correct only in septic shock with multiple risk features (eTG; eviQ).

options.text: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone lacks anti-pseudomonal cover and is inadequate empirical therapy in high-risk neutropenic sepsis. The anti-pattern is using community-acquired-pneumonia drugs in neutropenic sepsis. Ceftriaxone is correct in non-neutropenic CAP, not febrile neutropenia (eTG).

options.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours after cultures
options.rationale: First-line empirical therapy for high-risk febrile neutropenia in Australia is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours (or cefepime); broad gram-negative cover including Pseudomonas. Cultures drawn first. Add vancomycin only if line infection, skin/soft tissue infection or haemodynamic instability suspected (eTG Antibiotic; eviQ).

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is fever (single 38.5 or two 38.0 readings an hour apart) plus ANC under 0.5 x 10^9/L, and is treated as septic shock until proven otherwise. The Australian standard is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours after blood cultures, with cefepime as the second-line option when pip-tazo is contraindicated. Vancomycin is added only with line infection, skin or soft tissue involvement, pneumonia, haemodynamic instability or known MRSA colonisation. Antifungal cover (caspofungin or anidulafungin) is added at 72-96 hours of persistent fever despite broad-spectrum therapy. Risk-stratify with MASCC score: low-risk outpatients (MASCC over 21, no comorbidities, social supports) can step down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin per eviQ. G-CSF accelerates count recovery in selected high-risk patients but does not replace antibiotics.
key_points: Define: T >=38.5 once or >=38.0 over 1 hour with neutrophils <0.5
First-line: pip-tazo 4.5 g IV q6h (or cefepime)
Escalate to meropenem if persistent fever + shock
Add antifungal if fever persists 72-96 h
explanation.pearls: Empirical piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV within 60 minutes of febrile neutropenia recognition - cultures should be taken concurrently, never as a reason to delay antibiotics. Each hour of delay roughly doubles septic mortality (eTG; eviQ).

stem:
A 42-year-old previously well non-smoker presents to ED with one week of progressive facial swelling, neck swelling, dyspnoea and headache worse on bending forward. She has noticed dilated veins on her chest wall. She has had two episodes of pre-syncope in the last 24 hours. She has no haemoptysis or chest pain. On examination she has facial plethora, periorbital oedema, distended jugular veins to the angle of the jaw, dilated collateral veins on the anterior chest wall and a positive Pemberton sign.

Stridor is absent at rest. There is no airway compromise currently but she is sitting forward in bed and saturating 95% on 2 L O2. CT chest with contrast shows a large anterior mediastinal mass compressing the SVC with extensive thrombus. She has not been previously diagnosed with malignancy. Her FBC, U&Es, LFTs and LDH (elevated at 950) are pending tissue diagnosis.

data_table.Examination: Facial plethora, periorbital oedema, distended JVPs, dilated chest wall collaterals, positive Pemberton sign, no stridor at rest.
data_table.Investigations: CT: large anterior mediastinal mass compressing SVC with thrombus; LDH 950; no tissue diagnosis yet.

lead_in: In the absence of airway compromise or critical neurological symptoms, which step is most important BEFORE starting empirical corticosteroids?

options.text: Start dexamethasone 16 mg IV stat regardless of biopsy timing
options.rationale: Empirical steroids before biopsy are appropriate only with airway compromise or critical CNS symptoms; otherwise they transiently shrink lymphoma cells and obscure histology, delaying definitive chemotherapy by weeks. The classic 'steroids first' anti-pattern in stable SVCO destroys diagnostic yield. Steroids are correct only with critical airway/CNS features (eviQ SVC).

options.text: Start mediastinal radiotherapy empirically before tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: Empirical radiotherapy without histology obscures pathology, renders large areas uninterpretable, and the regimen depends on tumour type. Radiotherapy is correct only with life-threatening compression and no other options to obtain tissue, or after biopsy in confirmed tumour type (eviQ).

options.text: Obtain tissue diagnosis (core biopsy of accessible peripheral node or mediastinal biopsy)
options.rationale: In SVC obstruction without airway compromise or critical CNS symptoms, tissue diagnosis should be obtained BEFORE corticosteroids whenever possible because steroids can transiently shrink lymphoma and obscure histology, delaying definitive treatment by weeks. Anterior mediastinal mass + young non-smoker with high LDH = lymphoma until proven otherwise (eviQ SVC obstruction; BSH Lymphoma).

options.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation alone for the SVC thrombus
options.rationale: Anticoagulation may be added for SVC thrombus, but does not address the underlying tumour. The anti-pattern is treating the complication while missing the primary diagnosis. Anticoagulation is correct as adjunct alongside tissue diagnosis, not as standalone management (eviQ).

options.text: Endovascular SVC stenting as definitive management
options.rationale: SVC stenting provides rapid symptomatic relief and is appropriate for refractory or critical SVCO, but should not delay tissue diagnosis when the patient is stable. Stenting also makes subsequent mediastinal biopsy more technically challenging. Stenting is correct in critical SVCO not responding to chemo/radio (eviQ).

explanation.summary: SVC obstruction in a previously undiagnosed patient: get tissue diagnosis FIRST unless airway compromise or critical CNS symptoms force empirical steroids. Anterior mediastinal mass in a young non-smoker is lymphoma until proven otherwise, and lymphoma is curable with histology-directed chemotherapy (eviQ).
key_points: Stable SVCO: tissue diagnosis first
Critical SVCO (airway, CNS): empirical steroids +/- stent
Anterior mediastinal mass DDx: lymphoma, thymoma, teratoma, thyroid
Stenting and anticoagulation for thrombus
explanation.pearls: Steroids before biopsy can obscure lymphoma histology for weeks - delay treatment, not diagnosis.

stem:
A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with massive haematemesis. He arrives in haemorrhagic shock (BP 78/42, HR 142, GCS 13). The massive transfusion protocol is activated and he receives 6 units packed red cells, 4 units FFP and 1 pool of platelets via rapid infuser over 60 minutes. He is being continued on the MTP and IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes was given on arrival.

Repeat bloods now: Hb 78, platelets 62, INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L, potassium 6.2 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.84 mmol/L (RR 1.10 to 1.30), pH 7.18, lactate 8.4, base excess minus 12, magnesium 0.62, temperature 35.4 degrees C. ECG shows tall T waves in V2 to V4 with PR 200 ms; QRS 100 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/42, HR 142, GCS 13, T 35.4 (mild hypothermia).
data_table.Examination: Cold peripheries, ongoing haematemesis, jaundice, ascites.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (post-transfusion), platelets 62, INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1, K 6.2, ionised Ca 0.84, pH 7.18, lactate 8.4, BE -12, Mg 0.62; ECG tall T waves V2-V4.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate single next intervention?

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL given over 2 to 3 minutes via a peripheral large-bore cannula
options.rationale: Severe ionised hypocalcaemia (0.84) from MTP is immediately life-threatening because it depresses myocardial contractility, prolongs coagulation, and amplifies hyperkalaemia toxicity; ANZSBT MTP guidance recommends calcium replacement at every 4-unit interval and when ionised calcium falls below 1.1. Calcium also stabilises the myocardium against the concomitant hyperkalaemia, addressing two life-threats simultaneously (ANZSBT MTP; NBA PBM).

options.text: IV insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose is reasonable for hyperkalaemia, but with ionised calcium 0.84 and ongoing MTP the calcium deficit is the more immediate cardiac threat and calcium replacement also stabilises the membrane against the hyperkalaemia; insulin without calcium first does not address the broader hypocalcaemia (ANZSBT MTP).

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus to correct metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate does not correct lactic acidosis from hypoperfusion and acutely worsens ionised hypocalcaemia by increasing albumin-bound calcium fraction (ANZSBT MTP).

options.text: Active rewarming to address hypothermia as the priority complication
options.rationale: Hypothermia worsens the coagulopathy of the lethal triad and rewarming is essential, but it is parallel work; ionised calcium 0.84 with hyperkalaemia and ECG changes is the more immediate single life-threat (ANZSBT MTP).

options.text: Stop the massive transfusion protocol and reassess once haemodynamics improve
options.rationale: He remains in haemorrhagic shock with ongoing variceal bleeding; pausing MTP risks exsanguination. Metabolic complications are addressed alongside continued resuscitation, not by stopping it (ANZSBT MTP).

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion complications cluster as the 'lethal triad' (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy) plus citrate-induced hypocalcaemia and hyperkalaemia from stored cells. Calcium replacement is the most overlooked but critical intervention; ratio 1:1:1 of RBC:FFP:platelets reduces coagulopathy (ANZSBT MTP; NBA PBM).
key_points: Ratio 1:1:1 RBC:FFP:platelets
Replace calcium - citrate chelation is rapid and dangerous
Watch K+ from stored RBC; treat if symptomatic or >6.5
Add TXA (within 3 h) and target fibrinogen >1.5
explanation.pearls: Ionised calcium below 0.9 mmol/L is the silent killer of MTP - check and replace at every 4-unit interval.

subtopic_detail: Adult community-acquired sepsis: empirical regimen per eTG
stem:
A 72-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department with 36 hours of dysuria, rigors and increasing confusion. He has type 2 diabetes (metformin), benign prostatic hyperplasia (tamsulosin) and no documented antibiotic allergies. He was independent at baseline and lives with his wife. He has not travelled recently and is fully vaccinated. Triage observations show temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 26 per minute, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg and SpO2 95 percent on room air.

He is peripherally cool with capillary refill 4 seconds and a tender suprapubic region. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites, leucocytes and blood. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.31, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. Initial bloods reveal WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 14.1 x10^9/L, CRP 248 mg/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92), eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m^2. Two large-bore cannulae are sited.

Blood and urine cultures have just been taken. The team is preparing 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation per Surviving Sepsis. He is not pregnant, not neutropenic and has no indwelling devices.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 C, HR 118, RR 26, BP 96/54, SpO2 95 percent room air, CRT 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Confused, mottled peripheries, tender suprapubic, no flank tenderness elicited.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 14.1, CRP 248 mg/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92), eGFR 32, urinalysis nitrites+ leucocytes+ blood+.
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, tamsulosin 400 mcg nocte. No antibiotic allergy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen to commence within the next hour?

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose plus IV amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours
options.rationale: eTG empirical therapy for severe community-acquired urosepsis is a single dose of gentamicin (4 to 7 mg/kg IBW, adjusted for renal function) plus IV amoxicillin or ampicillin for enterococcal cover, pending culture (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV metronidazole 500 mg every 12 hours
options.rationale: Metronidazole adds anaerobic cover that is not required for urosepsis without intra-abdominal or genital tract focus; ceftriaxone alone misses Enterococcus. The anti-pattern is using intra-abdominal sepsis empirical cover for pure urosepsis. Ceftriaxone + metronidazole would be correct in suspected intra-abdominal sepsis or complicated cholangitis (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI).

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days after a single IV gentamicin dose
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy is inappropriate for septic shock with lactate 3.6 and AKI; severe sepsis mandates IV therapy until clinical and microbiological stability. Oral trimethoprim is correct as step-down or for uncomplicated lower UTI in non-pregnant adults with sensitive organisms (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours as sole agent
options.rationale: Pip-tazo is reserved by eTG for hospital-acquired or healthcare-associated urosepsis or where ESBL risk is high (recent antibiotics, known ESBL carriage, urinary catheter, recent hospitalisation). Broad routine use drives resistance. Pip-tazo is correct in healthcare-associated urosepsis or septic shock with broader risk (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV meropenem 1 g every 8 hours pending blood culture results
options.rationale: Carbapenems are reserved for confirmed or high-probability ESBL or severe sepsis after antibiotic failure; first-line empirical use depletes carbapenem activity (carbapenem stewardship). Meropenem is correct in known/strongly-suspected ESBL urosepsis or treatment failure (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Severe community-acquired urosepsis in an adult is treated with empirical IV gentamicin (single weight- and renal-adjusted dose) plus IV amoxicillin/ampicillin for enterococcal cover, alongside the hour-1 bundle - cultures before antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, lactate measurement and source identification (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid
eTG urosepsis empirical: gentamicin + amoxicillin/ampicillin
Reserve pip-taz and meropenem for hospital-acquired or ESBL risk
Lactate >= 2 mmol/L with hypotension defines septic shock
explanation.pearls: Source control matters - exclude obstructed system (renal tract ultrasound) early.

subtopic_detail: qSOFA, vasopressor initiation threshold and MAP target
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with diet-controlled type 2 diabetes presents from a nursing aged-care facility with 24 hours of productive cough, fevers and lethargy. Background includes COPD (GOLD 2, FEV1 62 percent), ischaemic heart disease with two coronary stents (aspirin, clopidogrel ceased 6 months post-PCI), and chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 110 micromol/L). She has no penicillin allergy. On arrival, T 39.1 degrees C, HR 124 bpm, RR 28 per minute, BP 84/48 mmHg, SpO2 91 percent on 4 L/min nasal prongs, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).

Chest examination reveals right basal bronchial breathing and crackles. CXR confirms right lower lobe consolidation. Initial bloods: WCC 21 x10^9/L, neutrophils 18.6, CRP 312 mg/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L, eGFR 24, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L. Blood cultures and a respiratory PCR have been collected. IV ceftriaxone 1 g and IV azithromycin 500 mg are running. She has received 30 mL/kg of compound sodium lactate (Hartmann) over 90 minutes.

Repeat BP after fluid resuscitation is 86/52 mmHg, HR 118, MAP 63. Urine output is 12 mL/hr. She has no signs of pulmonary oedema and JVP is not elevated. An arterial line and central line are being placed. She has an advanced care directive consenting to ICU-level care.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 118, RR 28, BP 86/52 (MAP 63) after 30 mL/kg, SpO2 91 percent on 4 L NP.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, mottled knees, CRT 4 s, RLL crackles, no pulmonary oedema.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 21 x10^9/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 110), bicarb 17, CRP 312, CXR RLL consolidation.
data_table.Medications: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV, azithromycin 500 mg IV running. Aspirin 100 mg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue further 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: After 30 mL/kg with persistent MAP <65, Surviving Sepsis recommends starting vasopressor rather than further indiscriminate fluid - additional bolus risks pulmonary oedema without restoring perfusion. The anti-pattern is fluid-fluid-fluid before pressor. Further bolus is correct only with clear ongoing hypovolaemia (rising lactate, falling JVP, fluid-responsive on POCUS) (Surviving Sepsis 2021).

options.text: Start IV noradrenaline infusion targeting MAP at least 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock with MAP < 65 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation; target MAP at least 65 mmHg, started through a peripheral or central line while lactate is monitored as a resuscitation endpoint (Surviving Sepsis 2021).

options.text: Commence IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day without starting a vasopressor
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is reserved for septic shock with ongoing vasopressor requirement, not as substitute for noradrenaline. Steroid alone cannot correct the perfusion deficit. Hydrocortisone is correct as adjunct after norad is established and ongoing pressor need >0.25 microg/kg/min (Surviving Sepsis 2021).

options.text: Switch antibiotics to IV meropenem 1 g 8-hourly before any vasopressor
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin is appropriate empirical cover for severe CAP per eTG; broadening to meropenem is not indicated and delays haemodynamic intervention. The anti-pattern is changing antibiotics when the problem is haemodynamic. Meropenem broadening is correct only with confirmed resistant organism or no source control (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells to optimise oxygen delivery
options.rationale: Transfusion threshold in septic shock without active bleeding or ischaemia is Hb 70 g/L (TRISS, TRICC trials). Transfusion does not address the core perfusion deficit and adds TRALI/TACO risk. Transfusion is correct only with Hb <70 g/L or active haemorrhage (Surviving Sepsis 2021).

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg with lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; further fluid bolusing after 30 mL/kg risks oedema without improving perfusion (Surviving Sepsis 2021).
key_points: Septic shock = persistent vasopressor need + lactate > 2 despite fluids
First-line vasopressor: noradrenaline
Target MAP at least 65 mmHg
Add vasopressin or hydrocortisone if noradrenaline-refractory
explanation.pearls: Lactate clearance, MAP, urine output and capillary refill are the key resuscitation endpoints, not a fixed CVP.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 12 hours of severe headache, fever, neck stiffness and one episode of vomiting. Her husband reports she has become drowsy in the last hour. Background includes systemic lupus erythematosus on prednisolone 10 mg daily and azathioprine 100 mg daily, and well-controlled hypertension. She has no penicillin allergy and is fully vaccinated, including pneumococcal and the recent meningococcal ACWY booster offered to immunosuppressed patients.

There has been no overseas travel and no household contact illness. On arrival, T 39.6 degrees C, HR 112 bpm, RR 22, BP 144/86 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent on room air. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). She has neck stiffness, photophobia and no rash. There are no focal neurological deficits, no papilloedema and no recent seizure. CT brain is being arranged before lumbar puncture because of her age, immunosuppression and reduced GCS.

Bloods are pending. Blood cultures have been taken. The team is preparing empirical antibiotic and adjunctive steroid therapy without delay. There is no clinical evidence of raised intracranial pressure. The Trust protocol mirrors eTG and Therapeutic Guidelines recommendations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6, HR 112, RR 22, BP 144/86, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck stiffness, photophobia, no rash, no focal deficit, no papilloedema.
data_table.Investigations: Bloods pending. CT awaiting. Blood cultures taken. No coagulopathy known.
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 10 mg daily, azathioprine 100 mg daily, perindopril.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical regimen to administer now, before CT or LP?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly alone after CT brain results, without Listeria cover or adjunctive steroid
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics must be given immediately without waiting for CT or LP; ceftriaxone alone misses Listeria - the key concern given age over 50 and immunosuppression. The classic anti-pattern is forgetting Listeria cover in over-50s or immunocompromised. Ceftriaxone monotherapy is correct in healthy adults aged 18-50 without Listeria risk factors (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV vancomycin 1.5 g 12-hourly plus IV meropenem 2 g 8-hourly without any adjunctive dexamethasone
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added only when penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is plausible (recent overseas travel to high-prevalence regions, prior beta-lactam exposure). Withholding dexamethasone is inappropriate because steroid before/with first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis (Cochrane meta-analysis). Vancomycin + meropenem without steroid misses both (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV dexamethasone 10 mg with or just before IV ceftriaxone 2 g and IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g
options.rationale: Australian therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in an adult over 50 or immunocompromised is ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly to cover Listeria, with dexamethasone 10 mg given with or just before the first antibiotic dose (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus IV aciclovir 8-hourly empirically, with no Listeria cover
options.rationale: Aciclovir is added when encephalopathy with focal features suggests HSV; the predominant syndrome here is meningitic, not encephalitic. Listeria cover is still required (benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin). Aciclovir is correct with confusion, personality change, focal neurology, or focal temporal lobe MRI changes (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Delay all antimicrobial therapy until lumbar puncture is performed to confirm the causative organism
options.rationale: Antibiotics must NEVER be delayed for LP when meningitis is suspected; cultures may take hours and untreated bacterial meningitis is rapidly fatal. The classic anti-pattern is investigation-before-treatment. LP after empirical therapy still provides useful information from cell counts and PCR (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: For an adult over 50 or immunocompromised, empirical bacterial meningitis therapy is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly for Listeria cover, with IV dexamethasone 10 mg given with or just before the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae in suspected pneumococcal meningitis. Do not delay antibiotics for CT or LP (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
key_points: Age > 50 or immunocompromised: add benzylpenicillin for Listeria
Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose
CT before LP only if reduced GCS, focal signs, immunosuppression
Empirical antibiotics never delayed for CT or LP
explanation.pearls: If LP is delayed beyond 4 hours of antibiotics, CSF culture yield falls but CSF Gram stain and PCR can still help.

sources.label: CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Invasive meningococcal disease

stem:
A previously well 34-year-old primary school teacher presents to the emergency department with three days of worsening headache, fever to 38.6 degrees C and now a generalised seizure witnessed by paramedics, lasting two minutes with full post-ictal recovery over 20 minutes. Her husband describes 24 hours of out-of-character irritability, word-finding difficulty and difficulty naming family pets. She has no past medical history, takes no regular medications, has no allergies and is up to date with vaccinations.

There has been no overseas travel, no animal bites and no household sick contacts. On examination she is afebrile post-paracetamol, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), with expressive dysphasia, mild right pronator drift and no neck stiffness. There is no rash. Vital signs HR 96, BP 132/78, SpO2 98 percent. A non-contrast CT brain is normal. LP cannot proceed for 60 minutes while a CT venogram is reviewed.

Bloods show WCC 9.8 x10^9/L, CRP 22 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. There is no coagulopathy. A consultant suspects herpes simplex encephalitis based on the temporal-lobe-pattern features.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 (peak), HR 96, BP 132/78, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, expressive dysphasia, right pronator drift, no neck stiffness, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: CT brain normal. WCC 9.8, CRP 22, sodium 134, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. LP pending in 60 minutes.
data_table.Medications: Nil regular. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Order MRI brain and EEG before initiating any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: MRI and EEG are useful diagnostic adjuncts (MRI shows temporal lobe oedema, EEG shows lateralised periodic discharges - LPDs/PLEDs) but treatment must not wait. Aciclovir is begun on clinical suspicion because every hour of delay correlates with worse neurological outcomes. Imaging is concurrent, not first (BMJ Best Practice: Encephalitis).

options.text: Wait for CSF HSV PCR result before starting any antiviral therapy
options.rationale: CSF HSV PCR may take 24-48 hours; empirical aciclovir must not be delayed. The anti-pattern is waiting for PCR confirmation in HSV encephalitis. PCR is sent but treatment starts immediately. PCR-first would be correct only in stable patients with low pre-test probability (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly as the priority therapy
options.rationale: Antibacterial cover may be added when bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded, but it does not treat HSV. Given the temporal-lobe encephalopathy pattern (dysphasia, behaviour change), aciclovir is the priority drug. Ceftriaxone alone is correct only with pure meningitic syndrome and no encephalitic features (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence IV aciclovir 8-hourly empirically without waiting for LP
options.rationale: HSV encephalitis presents with fever, focal temporal-lobe features (dysphasia, behaviour change) and seizures; treatment delay worsens neurological outcome. eTG and BMJ Best Practice recommend empirical IV aciclovir as soon as HSV encephalitis is suspected, before CSF results (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; BMJ Best Practice: Encephalitis).

options.text: Give IV phenytoin loading dose and observe for further seizures
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant load is appropriate for status epilepticus or recurrent seizures, but a single self-terminated seizure with full recovery does not require loading. The immediate priority is empirical aciclovir. Phenytoin load is correct for >5 minute seizure or >=2 seizures without recovery (BMJ Best Practice: Encephalitis).

explanation.summary: Empirical IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours should be commenced immediately on clinical suspicion of HSV encephalitis. Diagnostic features are fever, behavioural change, focal neurology pointing to temporal lobes and seizures. Delay worsens outcome; treatment is not contingent on CSF, MRI or EEG (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; BMJ Best Practice).
key_points: HSV encephalitis pattern: fever + temporal lobe features + seizure
Empirical aciclovir on clinical suspicion - do not wait for CSF
MRI typically shows temporal lobe oedema or haemorrhage
EEG: lateralised periodic discharges over temporal lobe
explanation.pearls: Treat for 14-21 days of IV aciclovir; renal dose adjustment and adequate hydration to avoid crystal nephropathy.

subtopic_detail: Empirical regimen and ECG monitoring for aortic root abscess
stem:
A 62-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement five years ago for severe aortic stenosis presents with three weeks of low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia and a 4 kg weight loss. He had a dental scaling six weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. On admission, T 38.2 degrees C, HR 92, BP 132/78. He has a soft early diastolic murmur not present at his last cardiology review.

There are two small painful nodules on his left index finger pad and a single splinter haemorrhage. There is no embolic stroke on examination, no skin emboli to soles. Two of three blood cultures drawn 12 hours apart grow viridans group streptococci. A transthoracic echocardiogram suggests mild aortic regurgitation; transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrates a 10 mm mobile vegetation on the bioprosthetic valve and an early perivalvular abscess. ECG on admission shows PR 168 ms with normal QRS.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, HR 92, BP 132/78, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur (new), Osler nodes left index finger, splinter haemorrhage. No focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: TTE mild AR. TOE: 10 mm vegetation + perivalvular abscess. Cultures: viridans strep x 2 of 3. ECG PR 168 ms.
data_table.Medications: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV 4-hourly + gentamicin per eTG. No allergies.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate additional monitoring step over the next 72 hours?

options.text: Weekly CT chest with contrast to screen for septic pulmonary or systemic emboli
options.rationale: Imaging for septic emboli is driven by symptoms, not weekly routine; CT chest weekly does not address the conduction-system risk in aortic root abscess. The anti-pattern is non-targeted surveillance imaging. Symptom-driven CT is correct when new pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, or focal neurology develops (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Single daily 12-lead ECG on the ward round, no continuous telemetry monitoring required
options.rationale: Daily ECG can miss intermittent or evolving block that develops over hours. Continuous telemetry detects evolving heart block in aortic root abscess - a high-yield surgical trigger. Daily-only ECG is correct in non-perivalvular IE without root involvement (BMJ Best Practice: Infective endocarditis).

options.text: Twice-weekly serum vancomycin trough levels for therapeutic drug monitoring
options.rationale: He is on penicillin and gentamicin, not vancomycin; gentamicin troughs are appropriate but do not screen for conduction-system extension. The anti-pattern is using TDM as a substitute for clinical surveillance. Vancomycin troughs are correct only when on vancomycin (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Daily transthoracic echocardiography to track vegetation size and perivalvular extension
options.rationale: Serial TTE has lower sensitivity than TOE for perivalvular extension and is not the recommended monitoring strategy; surveillance is by clinical examination, telemetry, and repeat TOE if features change. Daily TTE is correct only for tracking vegetation size in tricuspid endocarditis where TTE has adequate sensitivity (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Continuous ECG / telemetry to detect progressive PR prolongation or AV block
options.rationale: Aortic root abscess extends into the conduction system and progressive PR prolongation or new AV block predicts perivalvular extension and need for urgent surgery. Telemetry is mandatory until source is controlled (BMJ Best Practice: Infective endocarditis; eTG).

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed using the modified Duke criteria - definite IE requires 2 majors, 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Australian first-line empirical therapy for native-valve endocarditis is flucloxacillin plus benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; prosthetic-valve endocarditis adds vancomycin and rifampicin per eTG. Once organism is identified, narrow appropriately: viridans streptococci get penicillin plus gentamicin for 2 weeks (uncomplicated) or 4-6 weeks. Surgical referral early in admission is mandatory for any of: heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteraemia, abscess, fistula), high embolic risk (vegetation over 10 mm with prior embolism or anterior MV location), prosthetic valve involvement, or progressive conduction disease. Continuous telemetry catches the AV block of an extending perivalvular abscess earlier than daily ECGs. Repeat blood cultures every 48-72 hours until clearance, and transoesophageal echo within 5-7 days if initial TTE is non-diagnostic.
key_points: Modified Duke: definite IE = 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor
Perivalvular extension manifests as new AV block
Continuous telemetry until source control
Surgery indications include heart failure, abscess, persistent bacteraemia
explanation.pearls: In aortic-valve endocarditis, perivalvular abscess can extend into the AV node within hours; continuous telemetry for the first 5-7 days detects PR prolongation or AV block well before serial 12-lead ECGs do, and progressive conduction disease is an urgent surgical indication (eTG; AHA 2015).

stem:
A 27-year-old man who has sex with men presents to a sexual-health clinic 14 days after a single episode of condomless receptive anal intercourse with a partner of unknown serostatus. He reports 5 days of fever to 38.5 degrees C, sore throat, generalised maculopapular rash on the trunk, mouth ulcers, myalgia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. He is not on PrEP.

He has no past medical history and is on no medication. He is otherwise systemically well, alert, drinking and eating. There is no meningism. On examination, T 38.4 degrees C, HR 96, BP 124/76, multiple posterior cervical nodes 1 cm, palatal ulcers, truncal maculopapular rash. Bloods: WCC 4.1 with relative lymphopenia, ALT 92 U/L, AST 84 U/L, CRP 38 mg/L, EBV serology negative for acute infection, CMV IgM negative, monospot negative. He attends specifically asking whether he might have just acquired HIV, and the clinic is following ASHM guidelines for testing in acute infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 124/76, SpO2 99 percent.
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash trunk, posterior cervical LN, palatal ulcers, mild pharyngitis.
data_table.Investigations: Lymphopenia, ALT 92, EBV/CMV/monospot negative. STI screen pending.
data_table.Medications: Nil. Not on PrEP.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test for suspected acute HIV infection?

options.text: Antibody-only rapid finger-prick HIV 1/2 test as the sole screening investigation
options.rationale: Antibody-only tests miss the window period when antibodies have not yet developed; in acute seroconversion at 2 weeks the patient is typically antibody-negative but antigen-positive (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: A combined 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody test plus HIV RNA viral load
options.rationale: ASHM recommends 4th-generation Ag/Ab combined assays (which detect p24 antigen as early as 2 weeks) as the first test, plus HIV RNA viral load when acute infection is strongly suspected because antibody may still be negative (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: HIV Western blot as the primary screening test in suspected acute seroconversion
options.rationale: Western blot is a confirmatory antibody-based test, not a screening tool, and is also negative in early seroconversion (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: CD4 lymphocyte count alone as the initial diagnostic investigation in this presentation
options.rationale: CD4 monitors progression and informs prophylaxis thresholds; it does not diagnose HIV and may be transiently depressed by many viral illnesses (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Repeat HIV antibody test in 12 weeks before any testing now
options.rationale: Delaying testing forfeits the chance to start early antiretroviral therapy, which reduces transmission and improves immune outcomes. Test now with 4th-gen plus viral load (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents 2-4 weeks after exposure as a flu/glandular-fever-like illness with rash, mouth ulcers and lymphadenopathy. Diagnose with a 4th-generation Ag/Ab combined test plus HIV RNA viral load; antibody-only assays miss the early window. Initiate antiretroviral therapy immediately on confirmed positivity (ASHM).
key_points: 4th-gen Ag/Ab detects p24 from ~14 days post-exposure
Add HIV RNA viral load when acute infection suspected
Immediate cART benefits transmission and reservoir size
Contact tracing and partner notification follow
explanation.pearls: Rapidly start antiretroviral therapy in acute infection regardless of CD4.

subtopic_detail: Non-occupational PEP within 72 hours after high-risk exposure
stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents 36 hours after an episode of condomless receptive vaginal intercourse with a man known to be HIV positive on antiretroviral therapy. Her partner has been undetectable on viral load for 14 months on his last clinic letter, but she cannot reach him to confirm. She has no other STI risk factors recently, is on the combined oral contraceptive pill, has had a normal cervical screening three months ago, and her last HIV test (12 months ago) was negative.

She has no significant medical history, no allergies and normal renal function. She has not been on PrEP. She is anxious about acquiring HIV and asks specifically about post-exposure prophylaxis. The clinic follows the ASHM National PEP Guidelines. There are no contraindications to standard PEP. She is not pregnant on point-of-care testing. Hepatitis B serology is negative, hepatitis C antibody negative. She is up to date with HPV vaccination. She agrees to follow-up testing per protocol.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 118/72, normal otherwise.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Baseline HIV Ag/Ab negative (today), STI swabs sent, HBV/HCV negative, pregnancy test negative, creatinine 70 micromol/L.
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that PEP is not indicated because the source partner is reportedly virally suppressed
options.rationale: Even when source is reportedly virally suppressed, ASHM advises shared decision-making and PEP is typically still offered when suppression cannot be confirmed in real time (lab-confirmed undetectable on documented treatment). Recent guidance leans toward offering rather than withholding when in doubt. No-PEP is correct only with documented sustained viral suppression confirmed in real time (ASHM PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Commence two-drug PrEP (tenofovir-emtricitabine) daily and review HIV serology at 4 and 12 weeks
options.rationale: PrEP is pre-exposure; after a known exposure event the correct intervention is 3-drug PEP within 72 hours, not PrEP (ASHM PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Commence three-drug HIV PEP (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir) within 72 hours, baseline HIV and STI testing, and arrange ASHM follow-up
options.rationale: High-risk exposure with source HIV-positive of unconfirmed virological suppression mandates 3-drug PEP within 72 hours and ASHM follow-up.

options.text: Repeat baseline HIV serology in 12 weeks without commencing any antiretroviral therapy now
options.rationale: Waiting forfeits the window during which PEP can prevent seroconversion. PEP must be started within 72 hours of exposure; efficacy falls sharply with delay. Repeat-serology-only is correct after PEP completion (baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks), not as the primary intervention (ASHM PEP Guidelines).

options.text: A single intramuscular dose of cabotegravir as one-off post-exposure prophylaxis therapy
options.rationale: Long-acting cabotegravir is approved as PrEP (every 8 weeks IM after lead-in), NOT as PEP. Standard PEP is a 28-day oral 3-drug regimen. The anti-pattern is conflating LA-PrEP with PEP. Cabotegravir is correct only for PrEP in selected patients with adherence challenges (ASHM PEP Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Non-occupational PEP after high-risk exposure must be started within 72 hours and continued for 28 days with a 3-drug regimen, preferably tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir. Baseline HIV, repeat at 6 and 12 weeks. Counsel about ongoing prevention - PrEP if recurrent risk (ASHM).
key_points: PEP window: within 72 hours, ideally earlier
Regimen: TDF/FTC + dolutegravir for 28 days
Test HIV baseline, 6 and 12 weeks
Transition to PrEP if ongoing risk
explanation.pearls: Receptive vaginal/anal intercourse with HIV-positive source is a category-1 high-risk exposure regardless of stated viral suppression in many ASHM workflows.

subtopic_detail: QuantiFERON-TB Gold over Mantoux in BCG-vaccinated patients
stem:
A 28-year-old woman who arrived from Vietnam 6 months ago is starting a graduate nursing program at a metropolitan tertiary hospital. She received BCG vaccination in childhood. She is asymptomatic, with no fever, cough, weight loss or night sweats. She has no household TB contacts. She is not immunocompromised, not pregnant, and on no medications. Examination is unremarkable. Pre-employment screening with QuantiFERON-TB Gold returns a positive result.

CXR is clear with no parenchymal abnormality, no apical scarring and no calcified granulomata. She has no symptoms or signs of active TB on review. LFTs and HIV serology are normal.
