explanation.summary: TIA is a medical emergency. ABCD2 score helps risk-stratify but all TIA warrants urgent (same-day or within 24 hours) assessment with imaging, carotid evaluation, and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy for high-risk TIA or minor stroke.
key_points: ABCD2 score: Age, BP, Clinical features, Duration, Diabetes
Same-day specialist assessment for all suspected TIA
DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) 21 days for high-risk TIA / minor stroke
Carotid intervention within 2 weeks if symptomatic stenosis >=50%
explanation.pearls: Highest stroke risk is in the first 48 hours; ABCD2 has been criticised as imperfect but the urgency message stands.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents 2 hours after sudden severe headache, vomiting, and left hemiparesis. Non-contrast CT brain shows a 12 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage without intraventricular extension. He takes amlodipine for hypertension. He is on no antiplatelet or anticoagulant. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 198/112, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Imaging: 12 mL right basal ganglia bleed, no IVH, no midline shift.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate blood pressure target and timeframe?

options.text: Systolic blood pressure 140 mmHg within 1 hour using titrated intravenous antihypertensive
options.rationale: INTERACT-2 and ATACH-II support intensive lowering to SBP <140 mmHg in acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage within 6 hours of onset, reducing haematoma expansion. Use titrated IV agents (labetalol, GTN, clevidipine where available). Stroke Foundation endorses this target (Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines 2022; INTERACT-2).

options.text: Permissive hypertension - no antihypertensive treatment
options.rationale: Permissive hypertension applies to acute ischaemic stroke outside the lysis pathway; for spontaneous ICH the evidence supports active lowering to SBP <140 (Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines 2022).

options.text: Systolic blood pressure <100 mmHg within 1 hour
options.rationale: Over-aggressive reduction risks cerebral hypoperfusion in the perihaematomal penumbra; the validated target is 140 not 100 (Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines 2022).

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine produces unpredictable hypotension and is contraindicated in acute stroke (eTG Cardiovascular).

options.text: Lower over the next 24 hours to <160 mmHg
options.rationale: Slow lowering misses the haematoma-expansion window which is greatest in the first 6 hours; the 1-hour target is the validated approach (Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines 2022; INTERACT-2).

explanation.summary: Acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage benefits from intensive blood pressure lowering to SBP <140 mmHg within 1 hour, reducing haematoma expansion and improving functional outcome. Use titrated IV agents (labetalol, GTN); avoid sublingual nifedipine and over-aggressive reductions.
key_points: SBP target <140 mmHg within 1 hour
Window of greatest benefit is first 6 hours
Reverse anticoagulants (PCC + vitamin K for warfarin; specific reversal for DOACs)
Neurosurgical referral for cerebellar bleed, hydrocephalus, large lobar
explanation.pearls: INTERACT-2 was the practice-changing trial; ATACH-II tested lower targets without added benefit and signal of harm.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department after a witnessed first generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds. He bit his tongue and was post-ictal for 20 minutes. He has fully recovered. He drinks 4 standard drinks on Fridays and Saturdays. No illicit drug use. He works as a courier driver. Examination, electrolytes, glucose and ECG are normal. Non-contrast CT brain is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 124/72, T 36.8 C, BSL 5.4 mmol/L.
data_table.Investigations: U&E, glucose, calcium, magnesium, CRP, ECG normal. CT brain normal.
data_table.Driving: Class C licence; works as a courier.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient MRI brain and electroencephalogram (EEG), neurology follow-up within 4 weeks, no antiepileptic started, and advise non-driving per Austroads
options.rationale: After a first unprovoked seizure with normal examination, electrolytes and CT, the standard pathway is outpatient MRI and EEG to risk-stratify recurrence; antiepileptic medication is started only if recurrence risk is high (focal abnormality, epileptiform EEG) or after a second seizure. Austroads requires 6 months non-driving for private licence after first unprovoked seizure, 5 years for commercial (eTG Neurology; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022).

options.text: Start sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily and discharge with a 6-month GP follow-up, without outpatient MRI brain or electroencephalogram first
options.rationale: After a single unprovoked seizure with normal initial workup, antiepileptics are not routinely started; recurrence risk informs the decision (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Admit for 48-hour inpatient video EEG monitoring as the next investigation, deferring outpatient MRI and outpatient neurology review until after admission
options.rationale: Inpatient video EEG is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty between epilepsy and non-epileptic events or for seizure characterisation, not routine first-seizure workup (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Discharge with no neurology follow-up, no MRI, no EEG, and no specific driving advice provided that examination remains normal at the time of discharge
options.rationale: Failure to arrange neurology follow-up and imaging risks missing a structural lesion and leaves driving advice and recurrence-prevention unaddressed (Source: eTG Neurology; Austroads).

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis prior to discharge, despite the afebrile, alert and fully recovered status of the patient
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is indicated only when meningitis, encephalitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage are clinically suggested; afebrile, alert, fully recovered patients do not need LP (Source: eTG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: After a first unprovoked seizure, outpatient MRI brain and EEG inform recurrence risk and the decision to start antiepileptic. Provoked seizures (electrolyte derangement, withdrawal, fever) need treatment of the cause, not antiepileptic. Driving restrictions follow Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive.
key_points: MRI brain (higher yield than CT) and EEG outpatient
Antiepileptic starts at second seizure unless high-risk first-seizure features
Austroads: 6 months off private licence, 5 years commercial after first unprovoked
Educate on safety: no swimming alone, baths, heights, ladders
explanation.pearls: Mandatory reporting to driver licensing is the doctor's role in some jurisdictions; in NSW driver self-reports but doctor may notify if non-compliance puts public at risk (Austroads).

stem: A 19-year-old university student is admitted with confirmed invasive meningococcal disease (CSF and blood cultures positive for Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B). She lives in shared university accommodation with 4 housemates and attended a 5-hour party 2 days before admission with 12 other people. She is on appropriate antibiotics.

data_table.Background: Confirmed IMD serogroup B.
data_table.Contacts: 4 household contacts; 12 party attendees with prolonged close contact.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate public health response for close contacts?

options.text: Notify public health unit; offer ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally single dose (or rifampicin) to household and prolonged close contacts; arrange meningococcal B vaccination via public health
options.rationale: Invasive meningococcal disease is a notifiable disease in all Australian jurisdictions. Public health coordinates contact tracing and chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally single dose first-line; rifampicin or ceftriaxone alternatives) for household and prolonged close contacts within the previous 7 days. Vaccination of contacts is recommended for serogroup-specific exposure where vaccine is available (CDNA SoNG Meningococcal Disease).

options.text: Treat the index case only; contacts only need treatment if they develop symptoms
options.rationale: Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts within 7 days of index case onset reduces secondary cases; delaying until symptoms develop misses the prophylaxis window (CDNA SoNG).

options.text: Offer benzathine penicillin intramuscular to all contacts
options.rationale: Benzathine penicillin is not used for meningococcal prophylaxis; ciprofloxacin oral single dose is the AU first-line agent (eTG Antibiotic; CDNA SoNG).

options.text: Casual contacts (classmates, gym buddies) also require prophylaxis
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is for household, intimate, and prolonged close contacts only (>8 hours in confined space, sharing utensils, kissing). Casual contact does not warrant prophylaxis (CDNA SoNG).

options.text: Defer notification until microbiology confirms serogroup
options.rationale: Notification is on clinical suspicion or initial positive Gram stain/PCR - not after full serogroup characterisation. Delay forfeits prophylaxis window (Public Health Act NSW; CDNA SoNG).

explanation.summary: Invasive meningococcal disease is a notifiable urgent public health event. Chemoprophylaxis with single-dose ciprofloxacin for household, intimate, and prolonged close contacts within 7 days of onset reduces secondary cases. Public health coordinates vaccine offer for serogroups with available vaccines (B, ACWY).
key_points: Notify public health on clinical suspicion or initial positive Gram stain/PCR
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose first-line (or rifampicin 600 mg BD x 2 days, or IM ceftriaxone in pregnancy)
Prophylaxis for household, intimate partners, prolonged close contacts (>8 h confined)
Vaccinate contacts for serogroup-specific exposure where vaccine available
explanation.pearls: The index patient also needs chemoprophylaxis prior to discharge unless treated with ceftriaxone (which eradicates carriage).

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with 4 months of progressive proximal lower limb weakness, dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, and difficulty rising from a chair. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history. On examination, knee reflexes are absent at rest but become elicitable after 10 seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction. Strength initially weak but improves with repeated effort. No ptosis, no ocular involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 128/74, SpO2 97% room air.
data_table.Examination: Proximal LL weakness, areflexic at rest with post-exercise facilitation, no ocular involvement.
data_table.Autonomic: Dry mouth, ED, postural drop 22 mmHg.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography (CT) thorax and voltage-gated calcium channel antibody assay
options.rationale: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is paraneoplastic in 50 to 60% (most often small cell lung cancer) and identified by post-exercise facilitation, autonomic features, and proximal weakness. Voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies are diagnostic; CT thorax screens for underlying malignancy (eTG Neurology; ANZAN).

options.text: Acetylcholine receptor antibody assay alone, in keeping with suspected myasthenia gravis
options.rationale: AChR antibodies are for myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic); LEMS is presynaptic. Post-exercise facilitation, autonomic features and absent ocular involvement point to LEMS not MG (eTG Neurology).

options.text: Lumbar puncture for albuminocytological dissociation suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome
options.rationale: Albuminocytological dissociation is for GBS; this presentation lacks ascending weakness and post-infectious context (eTG Neurology).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to exclude a compressive cauda equina lesion
options.rationale: Spinal cord disease would produce a sensory level, bladder/bowel involvement and hyperreflexia; this is a neuromuscular junction picture (eTG Neurology).

options.text: Overnight polysomnography to investigate sleep apnoea contributing to weakness
options.rationale: Sleep study does not address proximal weakness with autonomic features and post-exercise facilitation (eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, often paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer). Distinguishing features from MG: proximal weakness predominates over ocular/bulbar, autonomic features (dry mouth, ED), absent reflexes that facilitate with sustained contraction, and antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels.
key_points: LEMS: presynaptic VGCC, proximal weakness, autonomic, post-exercise facilitation
MG: postsynaptic AChR, ocular/bulbar fatigability, autonomic intact
50-60% of LEMS is paraneoplastic - screen CT thorax for SCLC
Treatment: 3,4-diaminopyridine, immunotherapy, cancer treatment
explanation.pearls: Post-exercise facilitation (Lambert sign) is the bedside hallmark distinguishing LEMS from MG; reflexes return after 10-15 seconds of sustained contraction.

subtopic_detail: KDIGO eGFR/ACR matrix + KHA-CARI referral thresholds
stem:
A 64-year-old man attends his GP for a chronic disease check. He has type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension, and a BMI of 33 kg/m^2. Medications include perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, empagliflozin 10 mg, and atorvastatin 40 mg. He denies haematuria, frothy urine, oedema or new urinary symptoms and has had no recent illness, NSAIDs or contrast exposure.

He has never been seen by a nephrologist. Examination shows BP 142/86 mmHg, no peripheral oedema, normal heart sounds and chest. Fundi show background diabetic retinopathy. Today's results in stable conditions: serum creatinine 168 micromol/L (was 162 three months ago and 158 six months ago); eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2; urine albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR) on a first-morning sample is 42 mg/mmol, confirmed on a repeat sample two weeks later at 38 mg/mmol; serum potassium 4.6 mmol/L; HbA1c 58 mmol/mol; haemoglobin 128 g/L. He has had no episodes of AKI in the past year.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, BMI 33 kg/m^2.
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema, JVP not raised, fundi: background diabetic retinopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L (stable), eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2, urine ACR 42 mg/mmol (confirmed 38 mg/mmol on repeat), K 4.6 mmol/L, HbA1c 58 mmol/mol, Hb 128 g/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, empagliflozin 10 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in his renal management?

options.text: Continue GP-led care and recheck eGFR and ACR in 6 months without specialist input
options.rationale: KHA-CARI/Kidney Health Australia lists ACR persistently above 30 mg/mmol as an independent referral trigger, in addition to eGFR <30 or rapid decline. GP-only care at ACR >30 is below standard. The anti-pattern is anchoring on eGFR alone. GP-led care is correct for stable CKD G1-G3a with ACR <30 (KHA-CARI/Kidney Health Australia CKD Management in Primary Care 2024).
source_refs: KHA-CARI / Kidney Health Australia CKD Management in Primary Care 2024

options.text: Refer only if eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m^2 on the next test
options.rationale: Waiting for eGFR to fall under 30 delays specialist input on renoprotection and dialysis planning. The anti-pattern is using a single referral trigger when KDIGO/KHA-CARI list multiple parallel triggers. eGFR-only referral threshold is correct only if ACR is consistently <30 mg/mmol (KHA-CARI/Kidney Health Australia CKD 2024).
source_refs: KHA-CARI / Kidney Health Australia CKD Management in Primary Care 2024

options.text: Stop empagliflozin because the eGFR has fallen below 45 mL/min/1.73m^2
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors are continued for cardiorenal protection down to dialysis; empagliflozin is initiated at eGFR thresholds well below 45 for cardiorenal indications under PBS criteria. The anti-pattern is stopping renoprotective drugs because of stable eGFR. Cessation is correct only with acute haemodynamic deterioration, recurrent DKA, or symptomatic dehydration (AMH; PBS).

options.text: Stop perindopril given the modest creatinine rise and switch to amlodipine
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are renoprotective and should be continued unless creatinine rises >30% or potassium exceeds 6.0 mmol/L; his creatinine is stable and K is 4.6. The anti-pattern is reflexive cessation for any creatinine rise. Cessation is correct only with significant creatinine rise, hyperkalaemia >6.0, or symptomatic hypotension (Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - hypertension in CKD

options.text: Refer to nephrology for assessment given persistent ACR above 30 mg/mmol
options.rationale: He has CKD stage G3b A3 (eGFR 30-44, ACR above 30 mg/mmol). Australian primary care guidance is to refer to nephrology when ACR is persistently above 30 mg/mmol or eGFR is below 30, both as standalone triggers, to optimise renoprotection and plan for advanced CKD (Source: KHA-CARI / Kidney Health Australia CKD Management in Primary Care 2024).
source_refs: KHA-CARI / Kidney Health Australia CKD Management in Primary Care 2024

explanation.summary: On the KDIGO heatmap his stage is G3b A3, an Australian referral trigger by ACR alone. Continue ACE inhibitor and SGLT2 inhibitor, optimise BP and HbA1c, and refer to nephrology (Source: KHA-CARI 2024).
key_points: Refer if eGFR < 30, ACR > 30 mg/mmol, or rapid decline (KHA-CARI)
G3b A3 carries high CV and ESKD risk - colour red on KDIGO heatmap
Continue ACEi unless Cr rises > 30% or K+ > 6.0 mmol/L
Continue SGLT2i for cardiorenal benefit down to dialysis
explanation.pearls: ACR > 30 mg/mmol alone is enough - don't wait for eGFR to drop.

sources.label: KHA-CARI / Kidney Health Australia CKD Management in Primary Care 2024
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - hypertension in CKD

subtopic_detail: Iron repletion before ESA, KDIGO Hb thresholds
stem:
A 72-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m^2, secondary to long-standing hypertension and obstructive uropathy after pelvic radiotherapy) is seen in renal outpatients. She reports six weeks of fatigue and exertional dyspnoea climbing one flight of stairs. She denies overt bleeding, melaena, haematuria or menorrhagia (post-menopausal). Medications: amlodipine 10 mg, irbesartan 300 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, colecalciferol 1000 IU.

She does not take NSAIDs. There has been no recent infection or hospitalisation. Examination: BP 138/82, conjunctival pallor, mild ankle oedema, otherwise unremarkable. Bloods (today): Hb 96 g/L, MCV 88 fL, ferritin 78 microgram/L, transferrin saturation 14 percent, CRP 4 mg/L, B12 and folate normal, reticulocyte count low, creatinine 232 micromol/L (stable), eGFR 22, K 4.4 mmol/L, PTH 18 pmol/L, corrected Ca 2.30 mmol/L, phosphate 1.4 mmol/L. Faecal occult blood is negative on three samples.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, SpO2 97 percent on room air.
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, mild ankle oedema. JVP not raised. No abdominal mass; PR exam unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, MCV 88, ferritin 78 microgram/L, TSAT 14%, CRP 4 mg/L, retics low, eGFR 22, PTH 18 pmol/L, Ca 2.30, PO4 1.4.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in managing her anaemia?

options.text: Commence subcutaneous darbepoetin alfa and review Hb in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Australian and KDIGO guidance require correction of iron deficiency before starting an ESA. Functional iron deficiency (TSAT 14%) leads to inadequate ESA response and higher doses with associated cardiovascular risks. The anti-pattern is ESA-first without iron repletion. ESA is correct after iron stores are repleted and Hb remains <100 with symptoms (KDIGO Anaemia 2012/2024; KHA-CARI Anaemia 2023).

options.text: Give IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) targeting TSAT 20-30% and ferritin 100-500, then reassess Hb
options.rationale: She has functional iron deficiency (TSAT 14%, ferritin within absolute-deficiency range for CKD) and Hb 96 g/L. KHA-CARI and KDIGO recommend a trial of IV iron in non-dialysis CKD to target TSAT > 20-30% and ferritin > 100 microgram/L before considering an ESA, since many patients respond to iron alone (Source: KHA-CARI Anaemia 2023; KDIGO 2012/2024).

options.text: Trial oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and recheck iron studies in 3 months
options.rationale: Oral iron is poorly absorbed and tolerated in CKD 4-5 due to elevated hepcidin (driven by inflammation and uraemia); IV iron is preferred. The anti-pattern is treating CKD anaemia like nutritional IDA. Oral iron is correct only in CKD 1-3 with minor functional deficiency, particularly if dialysis is not imminent (KHA-CARI Anaemia of CKD 2023).

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells today and arrange outpatient ESA
options.rationale: Hb 96 g/L without bleeding or symptoms does not meet transfusion thresholds (typically <70-80 g/L). Transfusion sensitises potential transplant recipients via anti-HLA antibody development - a critical consideration in CKD progressing to transplant. Transfusion is correct only for symptomatic anaemia or bleeding (NBA Patient Blood Management Module 3).

options.text: Investigate for occult GI malignancy with colonoscopy before any treatment
options.rationale: Her pattern fits anaemia of CKD with functional iron deficiency; FOBT is negative and there are no GI symptoms. GI workup is reserved for unexplained IDA with red flags (weight loss, age >60, FOBT positive). The anti-pattern is endoscopy for any low ferritin regardless of context (Cancer Council Australia Colorectal Cancer Screening 2023).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Colorectal Cancer Screening 2023

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency must be corrected before ESA in CKD anaemia. IV iron is preferred in non-dialysis CKD when TSAT < 30% or ferritin < 500. ESAs are added only if Hb remains < 100 g/L after iron repletion, targeting 100-115 g/L (Source: KHA-CARI 2023).
key_points: Target TSAT > 20-30% and ferritin > 100 microgram/L before ESA
IV iron preferred over oral in non-dialysis CKD stage 4-5
ESA target Hb 100-115 g/L - avoid > 115 due to CV harm signal (TREAT, CHOIR)
Always exclude bleeding, haemolysis, B12/folate deficiency
explanation.pearls: Functional iron deficiency = low TSAT despite normal/raised ferritin; hepcidin-mediated.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Colorectal Cancer Screening 2023

subtopic_detail: Sequencing phosphate binder vs activated vitamin D vs cinacalcet
stem: A 58-year-old man with CKD stage 5 not yet on dialysis (eGFR 12 mL/min/1.73m^2 due to ADPKD) is reviewed in nephrology clinic. He is asymptomatic of bone pain or pruritus but has cramping. He follows a low-phosphate diet with the renal dietitian. Medications: amlodipine, irbesartan, atorvastatin, sodium bicarbonate 840 mg TDS, colecalciferol 1000 IU. He is not yet anuric. Bloods at today's visit (consistent with the trend over the last 3 months): corrected calcium 2.18 mmol/L, phosphate 1.95 mmol/L (rising from 1.5 three months ago), PTH 78 pmol/L (rising from 45), 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 142 U/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No bone tenderness; mature radiocephalic AV fistula on left forearm with good thrill.
data_table.Investigations: Corrected Ca 2.18 mmol/L, phosphate 1.95 mmol/L (rising), PTH 78 pmol/L (rising), 25-OH vit D 78 nmol/L, ALP 142 U/L, HCO3 22, eGFR 12.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine, irbesartan, atorvastatin, NaHCO3 840 mg TDS, colecalciferol 1000 IU.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in managing his CKD-MBD?

options.text: Commence oral calcium carbonate 600 mg with each meal as a phosphate binder
options.rationale: Calcium-containing binders add to overall calcium load and are associated with greater progression of vascular calcification in CKD; KDIGO 2017 specifically recommends restricting their use, particularly when calcium is near upper limit. The anti-pattern is using calcium-based binders in modern CKD-MBD management. Calcium carbonate is correct only in hypocalcaemia or low-cost-constrained settings (KDIGO CKD-MBD 2017).

options.text: Start oral calcitriol 0.25 microgram daily to suppress the rising PTH
options.rationale: Activated vitamin D analogues (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) raise BOTH calcium and phosphate via gut absorption; starting calcitriol with phosphate 1.95 mmol/L will worsen hyperphosphataemia and accelerate vascular calcification. Phosphate control must come first. Calcitriol is correct only after phosphate is controlled and PTH remains elevated (KDIGO CKD-MBD 2017).

options.text: Commence oral cinacalcet 30 mg daily as a calcimimetic
options.rationale: Cinacalcet (calcimimetic) is PBS-restricted to dialysis patients in Australia and lowers calcium; with corrected calcium already 2.18 hypocalcaemia is a risk. Cinacalcet is correct for dialysis-dependent secondary hyperparathyroidism with adequate calcium (PBS - cinacalcet; AMH).

options.text: Add a non-calcium phosphate binder (sevelamer) and reinforce dietary phosphate restriction
options.rationale: KDIGO and KHA-CARI advise lowering phosphate towards the normal range as the first lever in CKD 5 with rising phosphate and PTH. A non-calcium binder is preferred over calcium-based binders because of vascular calcification risk, particularly with a calcium near the lower limit (Source: KDIGO CKD-MBD 2017 Update; KHA-CARI CKD-MBD).

options.text: Refer urgently for subtotal parathyroidectomy given the rising PTH
options.rationale: Parathyroidectomy is reserved for severe medically refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH persistently >88 pmol/L despite optimal medical therapy) with hypercalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia or symptomatic disease. Medical therapy has not been escalated. Surgery is correct only after maximal medical management fails (KHA-CARI CKD-MBD).

explanation.summary: In CKD-MBD, control phosphate first using diet plus a non-calcium binder, then address PTH with activated vitamin D once phosphate is acceptable. Avoid loading calcium and avoid activated vitamin D while phosphate is high (Source: KDIGO 2017).
key_points: Phosphate first, PTH second in CKD-MBD
Non-calcium binders preferred (sevelamer, lanthanum)
Activated vitamin D raises phosphate - sequence after phosphate control
Cinacalcet restricted to dialysis in Australia (PBS)
explanation.pearls: Rising PTH with rising phosphate = give a binder before reaching for calcitriol.

subtopic_detail: AEIOU + advance care planning in frail older adult
stem:
An 82-year-old woman with CKD stage 5 (eGFR 8 mL/min/1.73m^2 due to renovascular disease and longstanding T2DM) is admitted with fatigue, anorexia and one week of intermittent confusion. She lives alone with package supports, has a Clinical Frailty Scale of 7, and a Charlson index of 9 (T2DM with retinopathy and neuropathy, IHD with PCI, HF with EF 35 percent, COPD).

She has been counselled previously about home haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis and has expressed a preference 'not to live on a machine' but has not formalised this. She is alert, oriented to person and place only. Bloods: K 5.4 mmol/L, HCO3 19 mmol/L, urea 38 mmol/L, creatinine 412 micromol/L, Hb 92 g/L, no acidaemia on VBG (pH 7.34), no pulmonary oedema on CXR, urine output 1100 mL/day. She has not been exposed to NSAIDs, contrast or new nephrotoxins.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent on RA, T 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Mild asterixis, mild peripheral oedema, no pericardial rub. Clear chest.
data_table.Investigations: K 5.4, HCO3 19, urea 38 mmol/L, creatinine 412 micromol/L, Hb 92, pH 7.34, normal CXR, UO 1100 mL/day.
data_table.Medications: Furosemide 40 mg, amlodipine, aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin, gliclazide MR 60 mg, insulin glargine 14 units.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Insert a tunnelled vascath and commence urgent in-centre haemodialysis today
options.rationale: Her bloods do not meet AEIOU criteria for emergency dialysis (no severe acidosis, refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, uraemic encephalopathy/pericarditis, or toxic ingestion). Urgent dialysis bypasses stated preferences and provides no clear benefit in CFS 7 frailty. Dialysis is correct only with AEIOU criteria met and alignment with patient values (KHA-CARI Dialysis 2024).

options.text: Hold a formal goals-of-care conversation and offer renal supportive (conservative) care
options.rationale: In a frail older adult (CFS 7, Charlson 9) without acute AEIOU indications, evidence from Australian cohorts and the ANZSN Renal Supportive Care framework shows dialysis offers limited survival or quality-of-life gain over conservative care. The next step is to formalise her preferences and offer a structured conservative pathway with symptom-focused support (Source: ANZSN Renal Supportive Care 2022; KHA Conservative Pathway 2023).

options.text: Commence inpatient peritoneal dialysis training and discharge home on PD
options.rationale: Implementing PD without revisiting her stated preference 'not to live on a machine' is not patient-centred; PD requires significant manual dexterity and home support that CFS 7 status may not allow. The anti-pattern is offering modality without exploring values. PD is correct when aligned with patient values and capability (ANZSN Renal Supportive Care 2022).

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for accurate urine output then discharge with GP review
options.rationale: Catheterisation does not address her uraemic symptoms or the need for a values-based conversation, and it adds CAUTI risk; her urine output is already documented. The anti-pattern is procedural action substituting for shared decision-making. IDC is correct only for urinary retention or accurate output monitoring in acute decompensation (ANZSN Renal Supportive Care 2022).

options.text: Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells targeting Hb 110 g/L to relieve her fatigue
options.rationale: Hb 92 g/L without bleeding or haemodynamic compromise does not meet transfusion thresholds and risks fluid overload (already 3 L positive) and transplant sensitisation. Iron studies and ESA optimisation are standard. Transfusion is correct only for symptomatic anaemia, active bleeding, or Hb <70 in stable patients (NBA Patient Blood Management Module 3).

explanation.summary: The decision to start kidney replacement therapy in CKD-5 weighs absolute clinical indications against frailty, comorbidities and patient values. Absolute indications use the AEIOU mnemonic: acidosis refractory to bicarbonate, electrolyte derangement (especially refractory hyperkalaemia), intoxication (lithium, salicylate, ethylene glycol, methanol, metformin), refractory fluid overload, and uraemic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy, intractable nausea, bleeding). In frail older adults without these absolute indications, ANZSN-endorsed renal supportive care offers structured symptom management, anaemia and bone-mineral therapy, advance care planning, and palliative care liaison - and is associated with comparable survival but better quality of life than dialysis in patients with Clinical Frailty Scale 7-9. Choice of in-centre haemodialysis versus home haemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis depends on lifestyle, social supports, vascular access and patient preference. A documented goals-of-care discussion involving family and renal supportive care team is the standard of practice.
key_points: AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes (refractory K), Ingestion (toxin), Overload, Uraemia (pericarditis/encephalopathy)
CFS 7 + Charlson 9 = frail; dialysis survival benefit limited
Document an advance care directive in NSW/Vic statutory form
Renal Supportive Care is an active treatment, not 'nothing'
explanation.pearls: In frail older adults with CKD-5 but no absolute AEIOU dialysis indication, conservative care matches or exceeds dialysis on quality-adjusted life-years and symptom burden - 'not starting dialysis' is a positive decision that needs a documented goals-of-care conversation and palliative care input (ANZSN 2022).

subtopic_detail: Pre-renal vs intrinsic - urine sodium and FENa interpretation
stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to ED with five days of vomiting, diarrhoea and reduced oral intake after a community gastroenteritis outbreak. Past history: hypertension, T2DM, IHD with previous CABG. Medications: perindopril 8 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, empagliflozin 10 mg (held 48 hours ago by his GP), atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg. He has not taken any NSAIDs or had recent imaging contrast.

On arrival: BP 96/58 mmHg lying, 78/44 mmHg sitting, HR 112, dry mucous membranes, JVP not visible, no peripheral oedema, soft non-tender abdomen, bladder not palpable. Bloods: Na 148 mmol/L, K 4.0, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 88 three months ago), eGFR 28, HCO3 19, lactate 2.4, glucose 9 mmol/L, CRP 12. Urinalysis: SG 1.030, no blood, no protein. Spot urine: sodium 8 mmol/L, urine creatinine 12 mmol/L, urine osmolality 612 mOsm/kg. Renal tract US: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 lying, 78/44 sitting, HR 112, T 36.6.
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, JVP flat, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Urea 22, Cr 198 (baseline 88), urine Na 8, urine osm 612, FENa < 1%, US normal, no obstruction.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, indapamide, metformin, empagliflozin (held), aspirin, atorvastatin.

lead_in: Which finding best supports a pre-renal aetiology over established acute tubular necrosis?

options.text: Postural hypotension on arrival with dry mucous membranes on examination
options.rationale: Orthostasis indicates volume depletion that explains the cause, but pre-renal physiology can progress to ATN if hypoperfusion is severe or prolonged. The discriminator between pre-renal and ATN is tubular function on urine indices, not the underlying haemodynamic state. Postural drop is supportive but not discriminatory (BMJ Best Practice AKI 2024).

options.text: Creatinine has more than doubled from her three-month baseline value
options.rationale: A doubling of creatinine satisfies KDIGO stage 2 AKI but does not discriminate between pre-renal and ATN; both can produce the same magnitude of rise. The anti-pattern is using a severity marker as an aetiology marker. Creatinine doubling is correct for KDIGO staging only (KDIGO AKI 2012).

options.text: Urine sodium 8 mmol/L with FENa under 1% and concentrated urine
options.rationale: Intact tubules reabsorb sodium and concentrate urine when perfusion is low; urine Na < 20 mmol/L, FENa < 1% and urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg are characteristic of pre-renal AKI. ATN shows urine Na > 40, FENa > 2% and isosthenuric urine (~ 300) due to lost concentrating ability (Source: BMJ Best Practice AKI 2024; KDIGO AKI 2012).

options.text: Hypernatraemia (sodium 148 mmol/L) reflecting a free water deficit clinically
options.rationale: Hypernatraemia reflects free water deficit, supporting hypovolaemia, but it is not a discriminator between pre-renal AKI and ATN - both can occur in a dehydrated patient. The anti-pattern is using a volume-status marker as a tubular-function marker. Hypernatraemia is correct as evidence of dehydration, not as aetiology of AKI (BMJ Best Practice AKI 2024).

options.text: Absence of hydronephrosis on bedside renal tract ultrasound today
options.rationale: Absence of hydronephrosis rules out post-renal obstruction; it does not distinguish pre-renal from intrinsic causes. The anti-pattern is treating exclusion of one cause as confirmation of another. Negative ultrasound is correct for excluding obstruction, not as a positive discriminator between pre-renal and ATN (BMJ Best Practice AKI 2024).

explanation.summary: Pre-renal AKI and acute tubular necrosis sit on a continuum: sustained renal hypoperfusion progresses from intact tubular function (pre-renal, fully reversible with volume restoration) to ischaemic tubular injury (ATN, days to weeks for recovery). Bedside discriminators favour pre-renal: BUN to creatinine ratio over 20, urine osmolality over 500 mOsm/kg (concentrated urine), urine sodium under 20 mmol/L, FENa under 1% (in oliguric AKI without diuretics), and bland urinary sediment. ATN shows muddy-brown granular casts, FENa over 2%, urine sodium over 40 mmol/L, and a more dilute urine. Diuretics confound urine sodium and FENa, so substitute fractional excretion of urea - under 35% favours pre-renal. Management is targeted volume restoration with crystalloid in pre-renal, withdrawal of nephrotoxins, and supportive care for ATN; no specific therapy hastens tubular recovery.
key_points: Pre-renal: urine Na < 20, FENa < 1%, U osm > 500, BUN:Cr > 20:1
ATN: urine Na > 40, FENa > 2%, U osm ~ 300 (isosthenuric), muddy brown casts
FENa unreliable on diuretics - use FEUrea (< 35% favours pre-renal)
Reverse cause: hold ACEi/diuretics/SGLT2i, replace volume, recheck
explanation.pearls: Fractional excretion of sodium under 1% in oliguric AKI without recent diuretics points to pre-renal aetiology; if the patient is on loop or thiazide diuretics, use fractional excretion of urea instead (under 35% favours pre-renal) (KDIGO 2012).

stem: A 71-year-old woman with CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2) and T2DM (HbA1c 56 mmol/mol) is scheduled tomorrow for an elective coronary angiogram for stable angina. She takes perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin and empagliflozin. She is euvolaemic on examination with no peripheral oedema, JVP not raised, clear chest, BP 134/78 mmHg, K 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L. She has no decompensated heart failure or current sepsis. The cardiologist plans iso-osmolar low-volume iodinated contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, clear chest, no oedema, JVP not elevated.
data_table.Investigations: Cr 132 micromol/L, eGFR 38, K 4.1, HCO3 25, HbA1c 56 mmol/mol.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin, empagliflozin.

lead_in: Which combined peri-procedural plan most appropriately reduces her risk of contrast-associated AKI and metabolic complications?

options.text: Continue all current medications and prescribe IV 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 mL/kg/h for 6 hours before and 6 hours after contrast
options.rationale: Volume expansion is correct, but metformin should be withheld around contrast in advanced CKD (eGFR less than 45) due to lactic acidosis risk, and SGLT2 inhibitors should be paused peri-procedurally given dehydration and euglycaemic DKA risk (KDIGO; AMH; ADS).
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society peri-procedural SGLT2i guidance

options.text: Withhold metformin and empagliflozin on the day of and 48 hours after contrast, give IV 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 mL/kg/h pre and post, and recheck creatinine before reinstating
options.rationale: KDIGO recommends isotonic crystalloid volume expansion in eGFR less than 45 receiving iodinated contrast; metformin should be withheld in eGFR less than 45 around contrast and restarted only after stable renal function; SGLT2 inhibitors are paused peri-procedurally per ADS guidance to reduce euglycaemic DKA risk (KDIGO; AMH; ADS).
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society peri-procedural SGLT2i guidance

options.text: Commence oral N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily on the day of and after the procedure, continue all usual medications
options.rationale: PRESERVE showed no benefit from NAC and KDIGO no longer recommends it; continuing metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor through contrast also misses important medication holds (PRESERVE; KDIGO).

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate infusion in place of normal saline, with IV furosemide 40 mg before contrast to maintain urine output
options.rationale: PRESERVE showed bicarbonate offered no advantage over saline, and forced diuresis with loop diuretics worsens contrast-associated AKI by causing volume depletion (PRESERVE; KDIGO).

options.text: Withhold all antihypertensives for 48 hours before angiogram and recheck creatinine on the day
options.rationale: Blanket cessation of antihypertensives is not evidence-based and risks uncontrolled BP; specific medication holds (metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor) are the priority while ACE inhibitor decisions are individualised (KDIGO; AMH).

explanation.summary: The mainstay of preventing contrast-associated AKI in CKD is peri-procedural IV isotonic crystalloid; NAC and bicarbonate are no longer recommended. Hold nephrotoxins (NSAIDs) and minimise contrast volume (Source: PRESERVE 2018, KDIGO 2012).
key_points: High-risk: eGFR < 45 plus diabetes; eGFR < 30 alone
Use isotonic crystalloid 1 mL/kg/h pre and post
Use lowest volume iso-osmolar contrast
Withhold metformin from procedure day until renal recovery confirmed; restart SGLT2i once stable
explanation.pearls: NAC and IV bicarbonate showed no benefit in PRESERVE - drop them from the bundle.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with two weeks of progressive ankle and periorbital swelling, weight gain of 6 kg, and frothy urine. He has no joint pains, rashes, recent sore throat, skin infection, or haemoptysis. He takes no regular medications. Examination: BP 138/86 mmHg, periorbital and bilateral pitting peripheral oedema to the knees, chest clear, no purpura. Bloods: albumin 22 g/L, cholesterol 8.8 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, eGFR over 90, normal FBC and LFTs, complement C3 and C4 normal, ANA and ANCA negative, hepatitis B and C and HIV negative, HbA1c 38 mmol/mol. Urinalysis: protein 4+, blood trace, no leucocytes or nitrites, no red cell casts on microscopy. Spot urine protein-creatinine ratio 480 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86, HR 78, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Periorbital + bilateral pitting peripheral oedema; chest clear; no rash.
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 22 g/L, cholesterol 8.8 mmol/L, Cr 88, eGFR > 90, UPCR 480 mg/mmol, urinalysis protein 4+ blood trace, C3/C4 normal, ANA/ANCA/HBV/HCV/HIV negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
options.rationale: In an adult with nephrotic-range proteinuria, normal complement, negative serology and excluded secondary causes (HBV, HCV, HIV, diabetes), the underlying glomerulopathy (membranous, FSGS, minimal change) cannot be determined without biopsy. KDIGO recommends renal biopsy in adult nephrotic syndrome where a treatable secondary cause has not been identified.

options.text: Serum and urine electrophoresis with free light chain assay to exclude paraprotein
options.rationale: Paraprotein workup is reasonable adjunctive testing in older adults or those with hypercalcaemia or anaemia, but in a 34-year-old with classic nephrotic syndrome and a negative initial secondary screen, biopsy will give the diagnosis faster (KDIGO).

options.text: Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) antibody titre as a standalone diagnostic test
options.rationale: Anti-PLA2R is highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy but a negative result does not exclude membranous (about 30 percent are seronegative) or other nephrotic glomerulopathies, so it cannot replace biopsy in adults (KDIGO).

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound with Doppler to assess kidney size and vascular flow
options.rationale: Ultrasound is part of pre-biopsy workup (confirms two kidneys, normal size, excludes hydronephrosis) but does not establish the glomerular diagnosis required to guide immunosuppression (KDIGO).

options.text: Empirical trial of high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and recheck in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Empirical steroid trials are reserved for paediatric minimal change disease; in adults this risks treating the wrong pathology (e.g. membranous, FSGS) and exposes the patient to corticosteroid toxicity without a histological diagnosis (KDIGO).

explanation.summary: Nephrotic = heavy proteinuria > 3.5 g/day + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema + hyperlipidaemia. Nephritic = haematuria with active sediment (red cell casts, dysmorphic RBCs), hypertension, AKI, sub-nephrotic proteinuria (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).
key_points: UPCR > 300 mg/mmol approximates > 3.5 g/24h
Nephrotic causes (adult): membranous, FSGS, minimal change, diabetic nephropathy
Nephritic causes: IgA nephropathy, post-strep, ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM, lupus
Next step: renal biopsy + secondary cause screen
explanation.pearls: Frothy urine + periorbital oedema in an adult should prompt UPCR and albumin, not just a dipstick.

subtopic_detail: ACR/UPCR treatment threshold and ACEi/ARB role
stem: A 27-year-old previously well man is referred to nephrology after two episodes of frank haematuria coinciding with a sore throat. Renal biopsy six weeks ago confirmed IgA nephropathy with mesangial proliferation and no crescents. He has no rash, joint pain or systemic symptoms. Family history of CKD is negative. Today, after 12 weeks of lifestyle advice and observation, his BP is 138/88 mmHg, eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73m^2 and stable, ACR is 78 mg/mmol (approximately 0.78 g/g; estimated 24-hour proteinuria 1.1 g) on first-morning samples on two occasions. Microscopic haematuria persists. He takes no regular medications. Hepatitis serology is negative.2 mmol/L. He has no signs of nephrotic syndrome and complement is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/88 mmHg, HR 72.
data_table.Examination: No oedema, no rash, no joint swelling.
data_table.Investigations: Biopsy: IgA nephropathy, no crescents. eGFR 78 (stable), ACR 78 mg/mmol (confirmed), microscopic haematuria, K 4.2.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures alone and recheck urine ACR in six months' time
options.rationale: ACR is well above the 0.5 g/day (UPCR ~50 mg/mmol) threshold at which KDIGO recommend initiating ACEi/ARB with BP target <120/70 in IgA nephropathy; observation alone is inadequate. The anti-pattern is watchful waiting in progressive proteinuric disease. Lifestyle-only is correct for proteinuria <0.5 g/day without other risk factors (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: Commence high-dose IV cyclophosphamide induction immediately without further investigation
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for rapidly progressive (crescentic) IgA nephropathy with crescents on biopsy and falling renal function. Not for stable disease with proteinuria around 1 g/day. The anti-pattern is escalating immunosuppression without histological indication. Cyclophosphamide is correct for biopsy-proven crescentic IgA (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: Commence high-dose oral prednisolone daily as first-line agent today
options.rationale: Systemic glucocorticoids are not first-line in IgA nephropathy; the TESTING and STOP-IgAN trials showed limited net benefit at general doses with significant toxicity. Steroids are considered only after maximal RAS blockade with persistent high-risk proteinuria, and increasingly replaced by targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon). Steroids are correct only after maximal RAS blockade fails (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: Refer for elective tonsillectomy as the patient's definitive disease-modifying therapy
options.rationale: Tonsillectomy is used in some Japanese practice but is not supported by KDIGO or KHA-CARI as routine intervention outside that context; western RCT evidence is lacking. The anti-pattern is generalising regional practice. Tonsillectomy is correct in Japanese guidelines for recurrent tonsillitis-associated IgA, not standard in Australia (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: Maximise ACE inhibitor or ARB, targeting BP < 120/70 mmHg and proteinuria < 1 g/day
options.rationale: First-line treatment of IgA nephropathy with proteinuria > 0.5 g/day is a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor titrated to the maximum tolerated dose with strict BP control (KDIGO target < 120/70). If proteinuria persists above 1 g/day after 3-6 months of optimised RAS blockade, second-line options (corticosteroids in selected cases, targeted release budesonide, SGLT2i) are considered (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021; KHA-CARI IgA nephropathy).

explanation.summary: IgA nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis in Australian adults, presenting with episodic frank haematuria coinciding with mucosal infections, or asymptomatic microscopic haematuria with proteinuria. Renal biopsy confirms mesangial IgA deposition and is also prognostic (Oxford MEST-C score). Management is layered: lifestyle (salt restriction, weight, smoking cessation) plus maximally tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB targeting BP under 120/70 mmHg and urinary protein under 1 g/day - these are the highest-evidence interventions and reduce ESKD progression by half. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) have Class I evidence in IgA with proteinuria and are second-line. Targeted-release budesonide (NefIgArd trial) is approved for high-risk patients with persistent proteinuria over 1 g despite optimised RAS blockade. Generalised immunosuppression has lost favour after STOP-IgAN showed no long-term benefit and significant harm. Tonsillectomy has no Western evidence base.
key_points: Treat if proteinuria > 0.5 g/day (UPCR ~ 50 mg/mmol)
BP target < 120/70 mmHg in proteinuric glomerular disease
Target proteinuria < 1 g/day after 3-6 months
SGLT2i added for additional renoprotection; budesonide targeted-release (Nefecon) emerging
explanation.pearls: In IgA nephropathy, maximally tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB targeting BP under 120/70 and proteinuria under 1 g/day is the first-line intervention - it halves the rate of progression to ESKD compared with proteinuria-tolerant management (KDIGO 2021).

stem:
A 64-year-old woman is admitted with three weeks of malaise, weight loss, sinus crusting and small-volume haemoptysis, on a background of two months of arthralgia. She has no history of smoking, no exposure to silica or solvents. Examination: BP 156/92 mmHg, saturation 95% on RA, scattered fine crackles bilaterally, mild ankle oedema, palpable purpura on the lower legs. Bloods on admission: creatinine 312 micromol/L (was 84 three months ago), eGFR 14, urea 28, K 4.8, Hb 96 g/L, platelets 380, WCC 11, CRP 124, ESR 92, albumin 28 g/L.

Urinalysis: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts seen on phase-contrast microscopy. UPCR 180 mg/mmol. Serology: MPO-ANCA positive, PR3-ANCA negative, ANA negative, anti-GBM negative, complement C3 and C4 normal, hepatitis B/C and HIV negative. CT chest: bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities. Renal biopsy is being arranged urgently.

data_table.Examination: Fine crackles bilaterally, palpable purpura lower legs, sinus crusting.
data_table.Investigations: Cr 312 (was 84), urea 28, K 4.8, Hb 96, CRP 124, MPO-ANCA positive, anti-GBM negative, urine red cell casts, UPCR 180 mg/mmol, CT chest peripheral GGO.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial induction regimen?

options.text: Oral prednisolone alone titrated to symptom control over weeks
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is inadequate for organ-threatening AAV with RPGN; combined induction with rituximab or cyclophosphamide is required to prevent ESKD. The anti-pattern is using only steroids in severe vasculitis. Steroid monotherapy is correct only in mild non-organ-threatening disease, never in RPGN (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone, plus rituximab (or cyclophosphamide), with PJP prophylaxis
options.rationale: Severe organ-threatening ANCA-associated vasculitis with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary involvement requires combined glucocorticoid plus rituximab (preferred in most settings, particularly women of reproductive age or where fertility preservation matters) or cyclophosphamide induction. PJP prophylaxis is standard during induction (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021; EULAR/ACR AAV).

options.text: Therapeutic plasma exchange alone as the sole intervention for induction
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is considered as adjunct in selected severe presentations (dialysis-requiring AAV, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage per PEXIVAS) but never as monotherapy; it must be combined with steroid + immunosuppressant. The anti-pattern is using TPE without backbone induction. TPE is correct as adjunct in DAH or rapid renal decline (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021; PEXIVAS).

options.text: Oral mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily as monotherapy for induction
options.rationale: MMF has a role in remission MAINTENANCE and in selected non-severe AAV (MYCYC trial showed lower remission rates than cyclophosphamide), but not as induction monotherapy in severe organ-threatening disease. The anti-pattern is using maintenance regimen for induction. MMF is correct for maintenance after rituximab/cyclophosphamide induction (EULAR/ACR AAV 2022).

options.text: Await renal biopsy result before starting any disease-modifying immunosuppression
options.rationale: MPO-ANCA-positive RPGN with peripheral GGO is treated empirically once anti-GBM has been excluded; delay risks irreversible loss of nephrons. Biopsy is arranged but must not delay induction. The anti-pattern is biopsy-before-treatment in time-critical disease. Biopsy-first is correct only when diagnosis is uncertain without ANCA positivity (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

explanation.summary: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, pulmonary haemorrhage, sinonasal disease and a constitutional prodrome over weeks. Diagnosis is by serology (PR3-ANCA cytoplasmic, MPO-ANCA perinuclear) plus tissue biopsy where feasible - but biopsy must not delay induction in organ-threatening disease. Induction is high-dose glucocorticoid plus rituximab (preferred for relapsing disease, fertility preservation, females of reproductive age) or cyclophosphamide. PEXIVAS established that plasma exchange does not reduce mortality or ESKD in most patients but remains reasonable for severe alveolar haemorrhage or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with creatinine over 300. Maintenance with rituximab 6-monthly or azathioprine for 24+ months; lifelong follow-up because of relapse risk.
key_points: Rituximab non-inferior to cyclophosphamide (RAVE, RITUXVAS)
Reduced-dose steroid regimen per PEXIVAS
Plasma exchange: selected severe disease, esp dialysis or DAH
PJP prophylaxis routine during induction (TMP-SMX)
explanation.pearls: Organ-threatening ANCA vasculitis is induced with IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for 3 days then oral prednisolone, plus rituximab 375 mg/m^2 weekly x4 (or cyclophosphamide); PJP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is mandatory throughout induction (KDIGO 2021).

stem:
A 38-year-old woman is admitted with three days of fatigue, easy bruising, and confusion. She had a vague URTI two weeks ago, denies diarrhoea, and is not pregnant (LMP one week ago). Medications: nil regular. No new drugs or supplements. Examination: T 37.8, BP 146/90, HR 104, GCS 14 (oriented to person, intermittent disorientation to place), petechiae on shins, mild jaundice, no lymphadenopathy.

Bloods: Hb 78 g/L with schistocytes on blood film, platelets 18 x10^9/L, LDH 1820 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, indirect bilirubin elevated, DCT negative, INR 1.0, APTT normal, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (was 70), urea 12, troponin mildly elevated, urinalysis blood 1+ protein 1+. Stool culture for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli has been sent but is not yet back. ADAMTS13 activity has been sent.

data_table.Examination: GCS 14, intermittent disorientation, petechiae, mild jaundice.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 + schistocytes, plt 18, LDH 1820, haptoglobin undetectable, DCT negative, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 3.2, Cr 142 (was 70), troponin mildly raised.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step before ADAMTS13 results return?

options.text: Await stool Shiga toxin PCR and ADAMTS13 activity before any TMA-specific therapy
options.rationale: Withholding treatment for TMA pending results is unsafe; untreated TTP carries >90% mortality. Empirical plasma exchange is standard of care when ADAMTS13 deficiency is clinically likely. The anti-pattern is investigation-before-treatment in a high-mortality disease. Await-results is correct only in stable patients with low pretest probability (ISTH TTP Guideline 2020).

options.text: Transfuse 1 unit of platelets to raise the platelet count above 50 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in suspected TTP can precipitate further microvascular thrombosis ('feeding the fire') and is contraindicated unless life-threatening bleeding or essential procedure. The classic TTP anti-pattern is transfusing platelets to a number. Platelet transfusion is correct only with life-threatening bleeding or pre-procedure (ISTH TTP Guideline 2020).

options.text: Start eculizumab as the first-line therapy for presumed complement-mediated TMA
options.rationale: Eculizumab is the treatment for atypical HUS (complement-mediated), suggested by predominant renal injury without severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. The clinical picture here is TTP-predominant. Eculizumab is correct only if ADAMTS13 is preserved and aHUS is diagnosed (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: Commence urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids for empirical TTP
options.rationale: MAHA + severe thrombocytopenia + neurological involvement + cardiac involvement + only modest renal dysfunction is the textbook TTP phenotype. ADAMTS13 results take time and TTP has > 90% untreated mortality, so empirical plasma exchange and steroids start immediately on clinical suspicion (Source: ISTH TTP Guideline 2020; BSH 2023).

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed sepsis-related disseminated intravascular coagulation
options.rationale: DIC is unlikely with normal INR/APTT and normal fibrinogen; the picture is non-immune MAHA + thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation - the TMA signature, not DIC. The anti-pattern is treating any thrombocytopenia with bleeding as DIC. Empirical antibiotics are correct in suspected sepsis-DIC, not TMA (ISTH DIC vs TMA review).

explanation.summary: TMA = MAHA + thrombocytopenia + organ injury. TTP: neuro/cardiac dominant, mild renal, ADAMTS13 < 10%, plasma exchange empirically. Typical HUS: diarrhoeal Shiga toxin (children especially). aHUS: renal-predominant, complement-mediated, treat with eculizumab (Source: KDIGO 2021).
key_points: PLASMIC score helps stratify TTP probability while awaiting ADAMTS13
Avoid platelet transfusion in suspected TTP
DIC ruled out by normal INR/APTT and fibrinogen
Drug-induced TMA (quinine, calcineurin inhibitors, gemcitabine) - withdraw the drug
explanation.pearls: Neuro signs + cardiac troponin + relatively preserved kidneys = think TTP, start PLEX.

subtopic_detail: Acute interstitial nephritis vs acute tubular necrosis
stem:
A 62-year-old woman is referred to ED with a creatinine rise noted on routine bloods. Six weeks ago she was commenced on a proton pump inhibitor for reflux and three weeks ago she had a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis. She reports a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on her trunk over the last week, intermittent low-grade fever, and mild fatigue. She denies vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, NSAID use, or contrast exposure.

Her usual medications are perindopril and metformin. Examination: BP 134/82, HR 84, T 37.6, mild non-blanching erythematous rash trunk and proximal limbs, no oedema, JVP not raised, clear chest. Bloods: Cr 198 micromol/L (baseline 70), eGFR 28, K 4.4, HCO3 21, eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L (raised), CRP 24. Urinalysis: blood trace, protein 1+, leucocytes 2+, nitrites negative. Urine microscopy: white cells present, no bacteria, no red cell casts; eosinophiluria reported on Wright stain. Renal tract US: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Examination: Non-pruritic maculopapular rash trunk + proximal limbs, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Cr 198 (baseline 70), eGFR 28, peripheral eosinophils 0.8, urine WBC + eosinophiluria, no casts, US normal.
data_table.Medications: PPI (6/52), amoxicillin-clavulanate completed 1/52 ago, perindopril, metformin.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and most appropriate next step?

options.text: Pre-renal AKI - hold the ACE inhibitor and rehydrate with IV crystalloid
options.rationale: Pre-renal AKI is supported by hypovolaemia, urine Na <20, concentrated urine; this patient is euvolaemic with sterile pyuria and eosinophiluria - not the pre-renal pattern. The anti-pattern is treating any AKI on ACEi as pre-renal. Pre-renal pattern is correct with documented volume depletion and low urine Na/FENa (KDIGO AKI 2012).

options.text: Acute tubular necrosis - give IV crystalloid resuscitation and observe with serial bloods
options.rationale: ATN typically follows a hypotensive, nephrotoxic, or ischaemic insult and shows muddy brown casts with urine Na >40 and FENa >2%; there is no haemodynamic insult here, and rash + eosinophilia + sterile pyuria fit AIN. The anti-pattern is missing the extra-renal clues to AIN. ATN is correct with appropriate insult history and muddy brown casts (KDIGO AKI 2012).

options.text: Pyelonephritis - commence IV gentamicin and ceftriaxone after blood and urine cultures
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis would show nitrites or bacteriuria, flank pain, and significant systemic features; sterile pyuria with eosinophiluria and no bacteria argues against UTI. Empirical aminoglycoside in AIN risks further nephrotoxicity. Pyelonephritis is correct with positive urinalysis and culture (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis - urgent biopsy and pulse IV methylprednisolone
options.rationale: RPGN presents with hypertension, oliguria, RED CELL CASTS, dysmorphic RBCs, and significant proteinuria. Sterile pyuria without red cell casts argues against a glomerular process. The anti-pattern is reaching for RPGN in any AKI with abnormal sediment. RPGN is correct with red cell casts + active sediment + nephritic features (KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021).

options.text: Acute interstitial nephritis - withdraw the offending drug(s) and consider corticosteroids if no improvement
options.rationale: The triad of rash, fever and eosinophilia with sterile pyuria/eosinophiluria after a new PPI and recent beta-lactam is highly suggestive of drug-induced AIN. Withdrawal of the offending drug is the cornerstone; corticosteroids are considered (typically prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg) if renal function does not improve within 7 days or if biopsy confirms AIN (Source: KDIGO AKI 2012; BMJ Best Practice AIN).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - Acute interstitial nephritis

explanation.summary: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) accounts for about 10-15% of biopsy-proven AKI, and over 70% of cases are drug-induced in modern Australian series. The triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia is present in well under a third of patients, so a sterile pyuria, white cell casts, mild proteinuria and a temporal drug exposure within the prior 8 weeks should prompt the diagnosis. Australian-relevant culprits include amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin, cefalexin, NSAIDs, PPIs, allopurinol, sulfasalazine, and the immune checkpoint inhibitors. First-line management is withdrawing the offending agent; oral prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks is added if creatinine does not begin to fall within a week or histology shows florid disease. Long-term renal recovery is incomplete in around a third of patients.
key_points: Eosinophiluria has poor sensitivity but supports AIN when present
Biopsy is definitive if doubt or no improvement after drug withdrawal
Common drugs: PPIs, NSAIDs, beta-lactams, sulfa, allopurinol, mesalazine
Consider steroids if no improvement at 7 days or severe presentation
explanation.pearls: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis from amoxicillin-clavulanate typically appears 7-14 days after exposure; PPIs cause an indolent picture over weeks with a normal-looking urine. Withdrawing the trigger is the highest-yield intervention - steroids only if creatinine fails to improve within 5-7 days (KDIGO).

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice - Acute interstitial nephritis

subtopic_detail: CK threshold, IV crystalloid, hyperkalaemia surveillance
stem:
A 52-year-old man is brought to ED after being found on the floor of his home approximately 18 hours after a fall complicated by alcohol intoxication. He has no head injury but is unable to bear weight on the left side due to pain. Past history: hypertension on perindopril, gout on allopurinol, harmful alcohol use. Examination: GCS 15, BP 132/82, HR 104, RR 18, T 36.8, SpO2 97% RA, dependent oedema and skin tenderness over the left thigh and calf, dark tea-coloured urine when catheterised.

Bloods on arrival: Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), K 5.6, HCO3 19, Na 138, urea 12, glucose 6.0, CK 84,000 U/L, troponin not elevated, lactate 2.6, AST 380, ALT 110. Urinalysis: dipstick positive for blood 4+, but microscopy shows no red blood cells. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no peaked T waves. He has not taken statins recently and no other myotoxic drug exposure is identified.

data_table.Examination: Tender left thigh + calf, dark urine, dependent oedema.
data_table.Investigations: CK 84,000 U/L, Cr 168 (baseline 88), K 5.6, HCO3 19, urine dipstick blood 4+ but no RBC on micro, ECG sinus tachy.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, allopurinol; no statin.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: IV furosemide 80 mg bolus to force diuresis through depleted tubules
options.rationale: Forced diuresis with loop diuretics is not supported and may worsen volume status and AKI; the goal is to expand intravascular volume, not to force urine through depleted tubules. The anti-pattern is forcing output before adequate input. Furosemide is correct only after adequate fluid resuscitation if pulmonary oedema threatens (Therapeutic Guidelines: Nephrology).

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis via a temporary vascath to clear circulating myoglobin
options.rationale: Myoglobin is poorly cleared by haemodialysis (large molecular weight); dialysis is reserved for standard AKI indications (refractory K, severe acidosis, fluid overload, uraemia) rather than myoglobin removal per se. The anti-pattern is using dialysis to 'clear toxins' when fluid resuscitation is the primary therapy. Dialysis is correct for AEIOU indications, not for myoglobin (BMJ Best Practice - Rhabdomyolysis).

options.text: Aggressive IV isotonic crystalloid (1-2 L/h) titrated to urine output 200-300 mL/h
options.rationale: The mainstay of rhabdomyolysis management is large-volume isotonic crystalloid to maintain urine flow and prevent pigment-cast nephropathy, plus aggressive monitoring and treatment of hyperkalaemia. Targeted urine output is 200-300 mL/h. Outcomes correlate with how early fluids are started (Source: BMJ Best Practice - Rhabdomyolysis; Therapeutic Guidelines: Nephrology).

options.text: IV mannitol 1 g/kg bolus to scavenge oxygen free radicals and force diuresis
options.rationale: Routine mannitol is not supported by evidence and risks volume overload, hyperosmolarity, and AKI in its own right; isotonic crystalloid is the standard. The anti-pattern is legacy mannitol practice. Mannitol is correct only in selected ICU settings with intracranial hypertension, not rhabdomyolysis (BMJ Best Practice - Rhabdomyolysis).

options.text: Restrict fluids and observe given a normal blood pressure on arrival
options.rationale: Fluid restriction risks pigment cast nephropathy and irreversible AKI; intravascular volume is contracted after rhabdomyolysis even with normal BP, and aggressive crystalloid is needed. The anti-pattern is anchoring on BP alone for volume assessment. Restriction is essentially never correct in acute rhabdomyolysis (BMJ Best Practice - Rhabdomyolysis).

explanation.summary: Rhabdomyolysis is muscle breakdown releasing CK, myoglobin and intracellular electrolytes into the circulation, defined biochemically as CK above 5x ULN (commonly over 1000 U/L) with myoglobinuria. Aetiologies include crush and trauma, prolonged immobilisation, seizures, drug toxicity (statins, fibrates, cocaine, ecstasy), heatstroke, infection, electrolyte disturbance, autoimmune myositis, and rare hereditary metabolic myopathies. Complications are acute kidney injury from pigment-cast obstruction and tubular toxicity (10-50% of cases, mortality 10%), severe hyperkalaemia (cardiac arrest), hypocalcaemia (calcium deposits in damaged muscle), hyperphosphataemia, metabolic acidosis, and compartment syndrome (which can be both cause and consequence). Management is large-volume isotonic crystalloid resuscitation titrated to urine output 200-300 mL/hour, continuous ECG and electrolyte surveillance, surgical fasciotomy if compartment pressures rise, and dialysis only for established AKI with metabolic or volume crisis - haemodialysis does not clear myoglobin.
key_points: Dipstick positive for blood + no RBC on micro = myoglobinuria
Watch for hyperkalaemia early; hypocalcaemia from Ca-PO4 precipitation
Hold/avoid nephrotoxins (ACEi, NSAIDs, contrast)
Mannitol and bicarbonate not routinely recommended
explanation.pearls: Aggressive isotonic crystalloid (1-2 L/hour titrated to urine output 200-300 mL/h) is the only intervention shown to reduce pigment-cast AKI in rhabdomyolysis; bicarbonate and mannitol have no proven benefit and add harm (Therapeutic Guidelines: Nephrology).

stem:
A 74-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m^2) and heart failure attends ED with malaise and palpitations. Medications: irbesartan 300 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, furosemide 40 mg, metoprolol, atorvastatin. He was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 days ago for a UTI. Examination: BP 138/82, HR 52 regular, alert. Bloods on arrival: K 7.3 mmol/L, Na 134, Cr 248 micromol/L (was 198 last month), HCO3 19, glucose 6.4.

ECG shows sinus bradycardia with prolonged PR, broad QRS approximately 140 ms, and tall peaked T waves in V2-V5. You have given IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes and the QRS narrows on repeat ECG.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, mild peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: K 7.3, Cr 248 (was 198), HCO3 19, ECG: peaked T waves, broad QRS 140 ms, prolonged PR.
data_table.Medications: Irbesartan, spironolactone, furosemide, metoprolol, TMP-SMX (5/7).

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate next set of interventions?

options.text: Repeat IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL every 30 minutes as the sole intervention, continue all current medications unchanged, and arrange urgent renal review for dialysis without further potassium-lowering therapy
options.rationale: Calcium stabilises the myocardium but does not lower potassium; repeated calcium without shift or removal therapy leaves the patient at ongoing arrhythmia risk once the calcium wanes (eTG Nephrology).

options.text: IV actrapid insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose plus nebulised salbutamol 10 mg, stop irbesartan, spironolactone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and arrange urgent renal review for dialysis
options.rationale: After calcium stabilisation, the priorities are shift therapy (insulin-dextrose plus salbutamol act synergistically), removal of the precipitating drugs (RAAS inhibitor, potassium-sparing diuretic, trimethoprim acts as a potassium-sparing diuretic via ENaC blockade), and arranging dialysis in CKD stage 4 with K 7.3 and ECG changes given temporary nature of shift therapy (eTG Nephrology; UK Renal Association 2023).

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g and IV furosemide 80 mg bolus as the shift and removal strategy, continue irbesartan and spironolactone at current doses, and admit for telemetry monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Cation exchangers act over hours, are GI-tolerance limited, and do not protect against arrhythmia in the next 30 minutes; furosemide is of limited utility at eGFR 22 and does not substitute for shift therapy (eTG Nephrology).

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes as the primary shift therapy, continue irbesartan and spironolactone at half dose, and arrange routine renal review at the next outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only modestly effective in non-acidotic patients and is not first-line shift therapy; continuing RAAS inhibitor and potassium-sparing diuretic in active life-threatening hyperkalaemia is unsafe (eTG Nephrology).

options.text: Withhold further potassium-lowering interventions, continue all current medications unchanged, and recheck the potassium in 4 hours, planning shift therapy only if it remains above 6.5 mmol/L
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is unsafe with K 7.3 and persistent precipitants in place; calcium effect lasts only 30 to 60 minutes and rebound arrhythmia is likely (eTG Nephrology).

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia management ladder: calcium (stabilise myocardium) -> insulin-dextrose + salbutamol (shift) -> diuretics, cation exchangers, dialysis (remove). ECG changes mandate calcium first regardless of the numeric K (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Nephrology).
key_points: Common culprits in CKD: ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, TMP-SMX (acts like K-sparing diuretic)
Calcium chloride 10% 5-10 mL via large vein if no central line for gluconate
Repeat ECG and K 30-60 min after intervention
Identify and treat cause; stop offending drugs
explanation.pearls: TMP-SMX raises potassium by trimethoprim blocking the ENaC channel - common, overlooked.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman is admitted from a residential aged care facility with two days of vomiting and reduced oral intake. She has long-standing heart failure on furosemide 80 mg daily and metolazone 2.5 mg three times weekly. Other medications include pantoprazole for several years, digoxin, perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination: BP 122/72, HR 96 with frequent ectopics, dry mucous membranes, no oedema.

Bloods on admission: K 2.6 mmol/L, Mg 0.55 mmol/L, Ca 2.30 corrected, Na 132, HCO3 32, Cr 142, eGFR 38, digoxin level pending. ECG: sinus rhythm 96, prominent U waves, occasional ventricular ectopics, QT prolonged at 480 ms. She has received 40 mmol of oral KCl slow-release tablets six hours ago at the facility but the potassium has not improved on the repeat venous sample. She is not on insulin and has no diabetic ketoacidosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72, HR 96, ectopics frequent.
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: K 2.6, Mg 0.55, Na 132, HCO3 32, Cr 142, ECG: U waves, QT 480 ms, ectopics.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in correcting her electrolytes?

options.text: Start an IV potassium infusion at 40 mmol/hour via peripheral cannula
options.rationale: Peripheral IV potassium should not exceed 10 mmol/h (max 20 mmol/h in closely monitored area); 40 mmol/h risks chemical phlebitis, cardiac arrhythmia, and is unsafe peripherally. The anti-pattern is exceeding safe peripheral concentration. High-rate K is correct only via central access with continuous cardiac monitoring (AMH).

options.text: Increase oral potassium chloride slow-release tablets to 80 mmol immediately
options.rationale: More oral potassium without addressing magnesium will not correct the deficit because urinary potassium losses continue while Mg is low (Mg keeps ROMK channels closed); large oral doses also risk GI side effects. The anti-pattern is treating the obvious electrolyte without checking cofactors. Oral K is correct as maintenance after acute correction (Therapeutic Guidelines: Electrolytes).

options.text: Replace magnesium intravenously (e.g. magnesium sulfate 10 mmol) alongside potassium replacement
options.rationale: Hypomagnesaemia drives renal potassium wasting through ROMK channel disinhibition; correcting potassium without correcting magnesium fails. IV magnesium repletion alongside potassium is the standard step. Loop diuretics, PPIs and metolazone are all magnesium-wasting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Electrolytes; AMH).

options.text: Stop pantoprazole and recheck potassium in 48 hours
options.rationale: Long-term PPI use contributes to hypomagnesaemia and should be reviewed, but stopping it does not address the current life-threatening hypokalaemia with ECG changes; acute replacement is required now. The anti-pattern is treating the cause without addressing the consequence. PPI cessation is correct as longer-term measure (Therapeutic Guidelines: Electrolytes).

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate for the alkalosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate would worsen the contraction alkalosis and drive K further intracellularly, deepening hypokalaemia. The anti-pattern is treating any acid-base abnormality reflexively without considering downstream effects on K. Bicarbonate is correct in severe acidosis (pH <7.1 or salicylate toxicity), not alkalosis (Therapeutic Guidelines: Electrolytes).

explanation.summary: Refractory hypokalaemia in any patient on loop or thiazide diuretics, with malnutrition, alcohol use, vomiting, or proton-pump inhibitor exposure should prompt an immediate magnesium check. Magnesium normally inhibits the ROMK channel in the distal nephron; when intracellular magnesium falls, ROMK opens and potassium pours into the tubular lumen regardless of how much potassium you replace orally or intravenously. The same patients are often hypocalcaemic too, since magnesium is required for PTH release and end-organ action. Replacement is intravenous magnesium sulfate 10-20 mmol over 30-60 minutes for symptomatic or severe deficiency, with co-administered potassium chloride and continuous ECG monitoring; oral magnesium oxide or aspartate is reasonable for mild outpatient repletion but causes diarrhoea at higher doses. Always recheck magnesium, potassium and calcium 6-12 hours after IV repletion.
key_points: Common offenders: loops + thiazides, PPIs, alcoholism, diarrhoea
Peripheral IV K+ max 10 mmol/h (cardiac monitored areas: 20 mmol/h)
Hold digoxin if level high or arrhythmias (hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity)
Always check Mg + Ca with K disturbances
explanation.pearls: Hypomagnesaemia disinhibits the renal outer medullary potassium channel (ROMK), so urinary K+ losses keep pace with oral replacement until magnesium rises above about 0.7 mmol/L - give 10 mmol IV magnesium sulfate before or alongside the KCl (eTG; AMH).

subtopic_detail: Rate of correction and osmotic demyelination prevention
stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of harmful alcohol use is brought to ED after being found drowsy. She has eaten poorly for two weeks. Examination: GCS 11, BP 110/70, HR 96, RR 14, T 36.5, weight 58 kg, mucous membranes moist, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurology.
